In every other case, they receive something for their money instead of the thing they would have preferred to buy had the choice been left to them. That is precisely how taxes work.

Regulations produce an effect very similar to taxation. Their ostensible purpose is to "help ordinary people" by restricting someone's choices somewhere. The truth, however, is that once all effects are accounted for, regulations at best benefit one group of people at the expense of others; more typically, they end up harming the very group they were meant to favor, and there are even regulations that harm practically everyone. A classic—and perhaps the most common—example of regulations meant to "help the poor" are all manner of product-quality mandates designed to protect poor consumers so merchants don't sell them "junk." Even if such a regulation actually achieved its stated goal without unintended side effects (which rarely happens) and simply cleared the market of low-quality goods, it certainly would not lower the price of higher-quality goods (quite the opposite, it would very likely drive their price up, since people who previously bought cheaper, lower-quality items are now forced to buy better ones, increasing demand and pushing prices upward). Thus, the biggest losers are precisely the poor whom the measure was supposed to help: stripped of the option to buy cheap, lower-quality goods, they often can no longer afford anything at all in place of that "junk." Someone might object that this situation "forces" them to wait rather than buy inferior items and later purchase something better—yet that brings us right back to the point made at the very start: no one can decide for those individuals better than they can themselves whether it is better for them to go without anything for a while so they can eventually buy something of higher quality, rather than having at least a lower-quality item the whole time (along with all the drawbacks that entails).

Another argument raised in favor of central planning (and thus against the free market) is the redistribution of wealth—the claim that the rich ought to pay for certain services for the poor. First, this changes nothing about what was just said: even if we grant the notion of such immoral and repugnant compulsory redistribution at all, the poor would still be far better off if the rich gave them that money directly and let them choose what to buy with it, rather than having someone else decide for them. More importantly, however, forced redistribution makes little sense in the first place, because wealth on a free market is a measure of how much a person has done for others according to their own scales of values. Top-down redistribution (and any coercive distortion of the market—not only by the state, though state distortion is by far the most common) thus favors people who are less useful to others at the expense of those who are more useful.

In closing, I would like to emphasize once again that understanding Chapter 2 and its subchapters is key to grasping most of the economic arguments throughout this book. A thorough yet accessible explanation of the phenomenon discussed here is offered especially in Ludwig von Mises's book "Bureaucracy"; for anyone who doesn't wish to read an entire book, I can recommend another angle on the topic in the excellent article "Neglected Economic Calculation" ("Opomíjená ekonomická kalkulace") by Petr Málek, one of the founders of the Ludwig von Mises Institute (freely available online). As a test of your grasp of this issue, try refuting for yourself a favorite argument of statists (supporters of the state): "If the state didn't pay for this or that, people wouldn't voluntarily spend money on it." Why can that claim never serve as a valid argument for preserving the state? Although this question will be answered in one of the closing chapters of the book, I sincerely hope every reader discovers the answer on their own before reaching it.

name: 3. The Non-Aggression Principle
text:
In the previous two chapters, we showed why the free market is generally better at satisfying human needs than state central planning. Many people are willing to agree with this, yet object that a free-market economy, while efficient, is heartless, amoral, unethical, and unjust. Is that really true? Does a big state really mean less efficiency in exchange for more justice? Let's break down and answer these questions.

Every human society in history has recognized some set of rules defining what is right and what is wrong. We call such a list of rules (statutes) law. Countless systems of law exist: customary law, the currently valid laws of the Czech Republic, the Code of Hammurabi, or, say, the legal code of the Third Reich. However, if something is legalized by statute, it does not necessarily make it moral and right—even if someone were to consider the laws of the Third Reich ethical, it is easy to see that different legal systems whose meanings contradict one another on fundamental moral questions cannot all be right at the same time.

What should "proper law" look like? A tough question. I will therefore try to summarize at least a basic minimum to which, I assume, most people would have no fundamental objections:

• No one should have the right to initiate violence against others.

• Everyone should have the right not to be robbed by others.

• The law should apply equally to everyone.

• The law should be clear and understandable; after all, if everyone is expected to live by it, they ought to understand it and keep it in their heads. The absurd thing is that although most people probably agree on this minimum, our legal system fails to meet even a single one of the points above.

The first point can be violated by the police. In some cases, for instance, when pursuing a criminal, the police have the right to forcibly commandeer cars from completely uninvolved drivers, or—even worse—to use those innocent drivers inside their cars against their will as roadblocks and human shields (relatively well-known cases took place in May 2011 on Legerova Street in Prague and in March 2013 on the D1 highway). Less obvious—yet far more frequent—violations of this rule are carried out by the police during house searches, taking suspects into custody, and the like. Whenever an innocent person refuses any of the above, the police are permitted to use violence against them.

The second point is violated by taxes, which are nothing other than robbery legalized by statute. The state says: "Subject, hand over the money, or else you'll be sorry—we'll take even more by force." It is essentially the same as a mugger telling us: "Your money or your life!" The only difference is that the state provides us with some service in return for that money, whereas a mugger typically does not. On the other hand, not only can a mugger hardly take so much from us (or so often), but above all, even if he bought us something with the stolen money, that wouldn't change the nature of the robbery, nor would he cease to be a robber because of it.

The third point is most blatantly violated by politicians with their parliamentary and other immunities, through which they tell us—to put it bluntly, straight to our faces—that we are not equal before the law. Furthermore, different laws apply to on-duty police officers (and other public officials) than to ordinary subjects.

The fourth point is particularly interesting in combination with the principle that ignorance of the law is no excuse. When even lawyers in disputes outside their own specialty routinely have themselves represented by specialized colleagues, there is probably not a single person in our country who knows all those rules thoroughly. Isn't the obligation to live by thousands of rules that virtually no one understands something you could write a genuinely hilarious comedy about—if only it weren't our reality?

The vast majority of the legal codes of almost all contemporary and historical states could be subjected to similar criticism. This is no coincidence. First, the very existence of the state contradicts equality before the law in principle (different rules must apply to representatives of the state than to its subjects), and second, the state must rob (collect taxes) in order to fund its own existence.

One of the few concepts of law that satisfies these (and many other) requirements—and at the same time probably the only one that respects private property and according to which certain human communities have broadly functioned over long periods in history—is called natural law. Throughout history, many philosophers have touched upon various aspects of natural law in their works: in antiquity, for example, Heraclitus and Aristotle, upon whose writings Thomas Aquinas drew in the Middle Ages, and among modern thinkers, John Locke. Most comprehensively and, in my view, best, it was described by my favorite author and thinker, Murray Newton Rothbard, in his book "The Ethics of Liberty" and partly also in his manifesto "For a New Liberty", where he formulated natural law as the so-called Non-Aggression Principle, which contemporary authors such as Walter Block and Hans-Hermann Hoppe write about in detail, while someone like Clint Eastwood summed up the Non-Aggression Principle very aptly in a single sentence: "Everybody leaves everybody else alone." I would describe the Non-Aggression Principle roughly as follows:

1. Ownership is a relationship that assigns physical objects to people (a person can be the owner of an object). No one may use or interfere with an owned object without its owner's permission, except when necessary to rectify a situation in which that owner has violated someone else's property or breached a contract.

2. Ownership can be freely transferred and exchanged provided both parties to the transaction agree (without violent coercion); transactions may be carried out through contracts.

3. Every person owns themselves until they transfer that ownership to someone else (some libertarians argue that self-ownership is inalienable; others—including me—hold that a person is free to do with themselves as they please).

4. Something that no one owns at a given moment can come to be owned by someone who begins using it (mixing it with their labor—so-called homesteading; see the work of John Locke). Homesteading addresses the issue of original appropriation: when something belongs to no one (such as newly discovered land and the like), anyone can acquire it by being the first to put it to use. The Non-Aggression Principle corresponds to a certain minimum of what most people consider right, moral, ethical, and just: it implies, in particular, that people should not rob one another, attack one another (though they may defend themselves), or kill; murder is a violation of the victim's property rights to their own body—and as the astute reader will surely have noticed, natural rights, formulated as the Non-Aggression Principle, are in fact property rights.

Although almost everyone agrees that the Non-Aggression Principle corresponds to a certain minimum of what is right, many object that it is not enough—that it would be moral for the law to include more things, such as essential medical care. Noble as such an idea may seem, incorporating it into the Non-Aggression Principle is simply impossible. Why? Well, someone has to provide and pay for that healthcare; if no one could be found to do so voluntarily, someone would have to be forced to do it by violence, which would violate property rights (and thus constitute aggression).

When we think about this more deeply, we find that adding anything else—no matter how noble—to this system of law contradicts its purpose or creates inconsistencies within it (which most legal frameworks contain anyway). Besides the right to healthcare, there is the right to education, a dignified life, a pension, housing—all these rights (when defined positively, i.e., not as "everyone is permitted to get an education," but as "everyone must be provided with an education") contradict the simple commandment "thou shalt not steal." I certainly do not mean to say that people shouldn't help one another; nobody should simply be forced to do so. In all known historical societies whose law was based on the Non-Aggression Principle, a considerable degree of voluntary solidarity existed (which makes sense: when you know you have a "right" to have someone help you in a crisis, you don't have to care much about others; conversely, when you depend solely on them, you will help if only so that you might receive help in return next time).

Despite the simplicity of the Non-Aggression Principle, one can derive from it answers to complex questions regarding, for example, freedom of speech, employment relationships, disputes over "public spaces," freedom of religion, and even traffic rules, carrying weapons, abortion, prostitution, and the governance of society in general (which states codify into thousands of impenetrable laws). Although anarcho-capitalism is fully consistent with the Non-Aggression Principle, this does not mean that the principle must be followed without exception in every situation in an anarcho-capitalist society, since there are no universally valid statutory codes. One of the favorite pastimes of statists is dreaming up improbable or even absurd scenarios that yield strange outcomes under a literal application of the Non-Aggression Principle, while completely ignoring the fact that if someone acts contrary to the Non-Aggression Principle yet in accordance with common sense and generally accepted ethics (which rarely happens anyway), people will probably accept their behavior (we will not encounter arbitrary punishment for completely understandable conduct on the grounds that "the law is the law").

Thus, although we cannot assume that everyone in a real anarcho-capitalist society would follow the Non-Aggression Principle unconditionally (after all, even the laws of today's states are not always obeyed), the two are connected as follows: first, anarcho-capitalism as a school of thought is derived from the Non-Aggression Principle; and second, in practice, in places where real (even if informal) anarchy prevailed during some historical period (such as medieval Iceland or the United States during the colonial era), society governed itself by rules very close to the Non-Aggression Principle.

Why the concept of law described above is sometimes called natural law is a rather philosophical question. Some claim that we all have it somehow hardwired into our brains (because it consists of property rights, and owning things is natural to humans) or that it is given by God. In my opinion, however, what matters more is that this law is moral, ethical, consistent, and non-arbitrary (applying equally to everyone). I leave the evaluation of these approaches to the reader—just as I leave the comparison of the Non-Aggression Principle with the law imposed on us by the state. It has probably not escaped anyone's notice that we have dealt only with the law as such, not with its enforcement—that is, putting it into practice; we will return to both of those in the fourteenth and fifteenth chapters of this book, while the next chapter will focus on the state's protection of the irresponsible.

name: 4. Supporting Irresponsibility Creates the Irresponsible
text:
"Whoever sacrifices liberty to gain more security loses both and deserves neither," said Benjamin Franklin, the eighteenth-century American thinker and scientist; I begin this chapter with that quote, as it will be devoted precisely to state interventions aimed at ensuring people's safety and protecting them. What can we say about such interventions?

From the first chapter, it follows that they are unnecessary; from the second, that they are ineffective; from the third, moreover, that they are immoral; and now, in the fourth chapter, we will show that—regardless of their unnecessariness, ineffectiveness, and immorality—the consequences of these interventions are negative for the very subjects for whose sake they allegedly exist.

First, let me list a few state interventions that promise people security in exchange for freedom, so everyone can picture what I am actually talking about: unemployment benefits, legal regulations on contracts "conspicuously disadvantageous to one party," welfare benefits, consumer and employee protection, and many others.

What is the problem? Well... aside from the fact that the market provides all of this better than the state (the general principles are described in the first two chapters, and we will address specifics in the chapters to come) and that it is immoral, because in order to provide any of the above, the state must first rob. Even if that weren't a problem for someone—what will people do when someone guarantees them (or creates the illusion of guaranteeing) that they cannot be cheated, that they cannot starve, that they will be provided for in old age, and that their children will always be taken care of? Well, they probably won't behave in the most responsible way.

One of the alleged "functions" of most states is supposedly to take care of the poor and helpless; naturally, this is carried out by forcibly compelling subjects to take care of others. To push this through smoothly, of course, it is necessary to keep instilling in people the belief that otherwise nobody would do it (Vladimir Putin perfected this in 2013, for instance, with his attempt to outlaw Yevgeny Grekov's charitable organization, which was "endangering the motherland" by building hospitals). Yet charitable societies existed even at a time when the state did not intervene in this area at all (details on how such societies functioned in the Czech lands can be read, for example, in the research of Professor Karel Engliš).

So what is the main difference between charity from voluntary associations and from the state? On the side of the payers, it is obviously a question of either voluntary generosity or being robbed; let us look, however, at the side of the recipients. Whereas voluntary associations carefully choose whom, how much, for how long, and in what form to help, the state guarantees a "right" to assistance. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk put it this way in 1919: "In the Czechoslovak Republic there will no longer be a place for the old charity, which was always regarded as an act of grace that always humiliated the poor recipient and dulled his human consciousness. In place of humiliating grace, today we put social duty."

Yet what is the natural consequence when a person in need does not have to ask for alms, when it does not humiliate the poor fellow, because it becomes his "right"? People will certainly have far fewer qualms about holding out their hand. Those who hold out their hand will then try far less hard to improve their situation. And above all, people throughout society will no longer worry as much about ending up in such a situation in the first place.

In discussions on this topic, many counter with: "Just look around you. Look at the people on the street. Look at those idiots who keep taking out vacation loans at absurd interest rates, care only about beer and TV, vote for Paroubek or Babiš in exchange for a free sausage or doughnut, and are incapable of taking care of themselves because they have no idea how the world works—they simply don't care, they couldn't care less. How are these people supposed to take care of themselves without the state?" Far better, I say! They don't care about anything simply because they have no incentive to. The state declares that it will take care of them; they believe it (and for the purposes of this argument it is irrelevant whether that is true), ergo they have no reason to bother. Economists call this phenomenon rational ignorance (when people believe the state is taking care of things, the expected benefit of learning some information about how the world works is often lower for them than the effort required to obtain that information).

Another example of rational ignorance is democratic elections. To make a truly informed choice among candidates, one would have to read election platforms and politicians' statements, familiarize oneself with each candidate's views, track their past record to gauge how sincerely they mean their promises, and so on. Such research takes on the order of dozens to a couple hundred hours. And what do you get for that time? Virtually zero chance that your vote will change anything, when everyone else is going to vote for whoever hands out a free sausage and beer anyway. Not bothering with it at all can then be a completely rational and logical choice.

Suppose you have a roof over your head and food to eat. You know that if you take out a loan you can barely repay, or if you lose your job, things will "work out somehow," and you'll probably still have a roof over your head and food to eat. What is your incentive to behave responsibly? Contrast that with a situation where you know that if you do something like that, maybe charity will help you once or twice, but after that you'll lose the roof over your head, you'll be cold, you'll go hungry, you'll lose everything. What is your incentive to behave responsibly now?

We see the consequences everywhere, including in the labor market. The modern state tries to increase the number of people with university degrees; the education system is structured accordingly, and standards are lowered—today practically anyone who puts in even a modest effort can get some kind of university degree. What does this lead to? On one hand, unemployment offices are flooded with social anthropologists holding degrees from some backwater college in Nowhereville, whose numbers exceed demand, so they cannot find work and therefore collect welfare. On the other hand, a computer programmer from Matfyz (Charles University's Faculty of Mathematics and Physics) posts a résumé online and is flooded with job offers within literally a few hours—not to mention that finding an electrician or a plumber is getting harder and harder because there are fewer of them than needed. That magical "how many are needed" refers to precisely the figure no mortal has any chance of calculating; the only answer is the market (the same rules apply in the labor market as in any other—namely, the principles we described in the first two chapters). This situation is a classic consequence of central planning in education, though it also has another cause: if we look at the average high-school senior choosing a university, they decide based on what they are good at and what they enjoy—or which school is easiest to slack through—while the criterion of "job prospects in the field" tends to be secondary and unimportant. The question is whether that would still be the case if they knew that studying a field for which there is no demand would leave them facing existential hardship, unable to start a family, and so on; the attitude of those students' parents would likely change accordingly.

Some will object: "Fine, but what about people who do try, yet are simply incompetent?" Much the same applies to incompetence as to lack of motivation. The world is a wonderful place, one of whose great qualities is an enormous degree of predictability: reach into a fire and you get burned; do it again and the result will be the same. This enables all thinking creatures to learn and develop; if the world operated completely at random, nothing of the sort would be possible. However, this predictability extends far beyond the laws of physics—it works quite well within socioeconomic relationships and, in fact, almost everywhere. Thanks to it, we can learn from our mistakes; yet when the state softens the consequences of those mistakes, it makes it harder for us to learn, thereby creating not only the irresponsible, but also the incompetent (not that they wouldn't exist without the state, though in far smaller numbers).

In general, then, the more the state supports the irresponsible and incompetent, the more of them there will be; and such people can hardly raise responsible individuals as children, so their numbers will grow with each generation and their dependence on the state will deepen. This creates an artificial argument for why the state is actually needed. Why artificial? The human instinct for self-preservation is still quite strong; the moment something is truly on the line and people are genuinely faced with the choice between starting to behave responsibly or starving and freezing, we can assume that most of them—for purely existential reasons—will prefer thinking over freezing (even though both hurt sometimes). And the more we buy into politicians' rhetoric that people cannot take care of themselves so the state must do it for them, the more we will see it become true around us; as soon as we say "no more," however, and stop subsidizing irresponsibility, we will witness its decline.

Inextricably linked to this is a phenomenon I call the "deadly cycle of democracy": a politician promises voters protection from the consequences of their mistakes; they elect him, he fulfills his promise (at least in part), and the state softens (obviously at someone else's expense) the negative consequences of certain bad decisions; being responsible starts to pay off less (the costs remain, but the price we pay for irresponsibility goes down), so there are more irresponsible people and more people dependent on the state (as well as more state employees carrying out the politician's promises); these people (and, in subsequent generations, their descendants) will typically vote for politicians advocating a strong state. Thus the circle closes: democracy inherently tends toward socialism, because it creates people dependent on the state—and all the more so the more such voters there are.

Certainly, however, I am not claiming that we shouldn't care for people in need (I do so myself in abundance); and history shows that those who care are not few—they simply choose for themselves whom to help and whom not to (typically, they do not help those who repeatedly get themselves into bad situations and make no effort to get back on their own two feet as soon as possible). The state, by contrast, claims that everyone has a "right" to assistance in need, which leads to a massive increase in dependents who don't even try very actively to solve their problems.

This chapter concludes the first part of the book, which deals with the general principles of human action, economics, the market, and the state. In the following chapters, we will examine individual areas of human activity that states currently hold in their grip by force. We will consider how they could function without violence, based on the actions of free people; in the very next chapter, we will focus on state-controlled money and banking.

name: 5. Money
text:
I will open this chapter with a well-known quote: "Give me the power to print and control money, and I will not care who makes the laws," attributed to none other than Mayer Amschel Rothschild, who, in my opinion, overlooked one very important fact when formulating this sentence; does it occur to any reader why Mr. Rothschild probably wouldn't really be indifferent to who makes the laws?

Almost all of us now perceive it as a completely natural thing, so we often forget that the state holds a forcibly imposed monopoly on money. What would happen, then, if Mr. Rothschild merrily started printing and controlling money, but those who make the laws repealed citizens' legal obligation to accept that currency? Probably what has happened in history practically every time the state gave people the choice, or whenever state money failed (typically too much of it was printed, leading to high inflation): private money spontaneously emerged on the free market, usually backed by a precious metal. People would rightly say: "Why should this Rothschild get to print money, devalue our savings, and live in luxury at our expense? Away with his money! Let's start using something else!"

In the first chapter, we described why and how money came into being. People exchanged goods and services with one another. When two people each owned something that was more useful to the other than to themselves, they voluntarily exchanged those goods, increasing the well-being of both without anything new having been produced. A complication arose whenever one person had something to trade that the other did not want; they then had to find a chain of people through whom to trade their goods (for example, trading bread for potatoes, which could then be traded for a steak, because the person with the steak had no interest in bread). First, this is complicated; second, it is not very clear which offer is most advantageous when several such exchange routes exist.

This problem was elegantly solved by the free market: some commodity spontaneously established itself as a universal medium of exchange. People began accepting it even when they had no direct use for it, knowing they would be able to trade it easily later. The prices of all goods were then expressed relative to this medium of payment. Examples of such universal media of exchange included, in particular, precious metals, iron, linen cloths, hides, grain, and many others. Naturally, these commodities continued to serve their ordinary functions (which, incidentally, made counterfeiting problematic: if the currency is grain, for instance, "counterfeiting" means growing grain—hardly a harmful activity, you simply become a farmer).

Over time, precious metals became established almost everywhere as money: they could easily be divided and melted back together, they did not spoil, large amounts of value could be stored in small volumes, and above all, their total quantity on the market only very rarely changed unexpectedly or in sudden jumps (for example, when a Spanish fleet carrying gold cargo sank).

Many people built their livelihood on metalworking: goldsmiths and jewelers, as well as coiners and minters of private money (people brought them their precious metals, which were processed at mints into coins stamped with their weight, making transactions easier since the precious metals no longer had to be divided and weighed each time). Over time, institutions operating in this field also began functioning as lenders and depositories: so that people would not have to carry precious metals around with them, they deposited them with trusted goldsmiths, from whom they received deposit receipts; they then began trading these receipts as if they were the precious metals themselves—and paper money was born.

Since the same institutions that issued receipts for deposited precious metals (i.e., paper money) often also made a living by extending loans, loans were frequently issued not as actual coins, but as these receipts (paper money). Naturally, this tempted individuals endowed with a higher degree of enterprise and a lower degree of morality to lend out more than they actually had. It was simple: the person issued receipts for more precious metals than he actually possessed. This usually worked until he went too far and rumors began spreading among the public. People then quite understandably started demanding precious metals for their receipts; the fraudster didn't have enough, and the game was up. He was dealt with according to local custom, which in the better cases meant hanging, and in worse ones burning at the stake, flaying, and similar pastimes.

As is often the case, when the state spots some wrongdoing, it doesn't take long before it establishes a monopoly on it. It was no different with lending out money that doesn't exist. In the vast majority of cases, the historical progression was roughly as follows: the state issued paper money as receipts for gold deposited in the state bank, then started a war it had no way to finance, and therefore printed more money than it had gold as a "temporary measure." Subjects were simply informed that state money was no longer backed by gold; naturally, this was not met with enthusiasm, and citizens preferred gold to worthless scraps of paper—which, however, usually posed little problem for the state, holding as it does a monopoly on violence: refusing to accept state currency was often punishable by death (or in some places "merely" imprisonment). Although at first it was always necessary to force unbacked state money on the people through violence, it wasn't all that difficult, over a few generations of brainwashing, to convince subjects that it didn't really matter; and a new method of legalized robbery was born.

How exactly does such robbery take place? In fact, in the exact same way as counterfeiting (except when the state counterfeits, it is called quantitative easing). If the money supply in the economy increases, its value falls, so prices rise (money is a commodity like any other; when there is more of it, it is less scarce, so its value drops relative to other goods—see the first chapter). Consequently, everyone holding savings in that currency transfers part of their value to the counterfeiter (the state, the banks). The nominal value of those savings remains the same, yet their owner can buy fewer goods with them, meaning their real value declines. Thus, when someone prints a billion crowns, they essentially steal everything they buy with that billion from all holders of that currency (who are robbed in proportion to how many crowns they hold).

Once state money had been forced upon the people through violence, the masses—with the help of heavy propaganda—gradually got used to it. Most states then eased their repressive tactics: although the law requires accepting state legal tender, in theory private currencies are not banned in many countries (they are, however, placed at a disadvantage because everyone is legally obliged to accept the state currency, and moreover taxes are collected in it). In practice, though, whenever someone tries to succeed in this market and begins doing well, the state finds a way to shut them down anyway.

In 1998, Bernard von NotHaus created the Liberty Dollar, a silver-backed private currency. Within a few years, over seven million US dollars' worth of silver (in the form of Liberty Dollars) had entered circulation, and the Liberty Dollar was growing increasingly popular. The United States government was alarmed by the potential competition, so it had to be nipped in the bud. In 2007, the FBI raided NotHaus; in 2009 he was indicted, and in 2011 he was sentenced to 25 years in prison (the trial lasted a mere 90 minutes) for conspiracy and counterfeiting. The conspiracy consisted in creating competition for the US dollar, and the alleged counterfeiting was even more absurd: one of NotHaus's coins supposedly resembled a US quarter (even though the quarter features a man's likeness and the Liberty Dollar a woman's); and even if a resemblance had existed, the alleged "counterfeit" made of silver was worth 160 times more than the quarter it was supposedly counterfeiting. Imagine expecting a quarter, and a wicked counterfeiter slips you a coin worth 160 times as much—$40; wouldn't that make you furious?

And so Bernard von NotHaus became yet another victim of the regime; although he was released after several years, the government had sent a clear message. From him—and from his innocent customers—the state simply seized all the Liberty Dollars by force. And what did Bernard von NotHaus actually do? What crime did he commit? He minted silver coins and sold them. Nobody was forced to buy those coins. The man was merely satisfying market demand, nothing more. Whom did he harm? Nobody. Unlike illegal drugs, which the government bans under the pretext of protecting us from ourselves, these silver coins did not harm even their own owners (on the contrary, it was the government that harmed them by confiscating their Liberty Dollars); they merely gave people a choice of what to do with their money. Why, then, do governments around the world usurp a monopoly on money? Well, simply so they can rob their subjects. There truly is no other reason here; one cannot even claim they are protecting citizens from anything. Free entrepreneurs operated in the money market for hundreds of years to everyone's satisfaction; then states spotted another way to subtly rob their subjects and immediately seized upon it.

In conclusion, it should be added that states usually do not carry out these monetary machinations themselves, lest it be too blatant. In reality, they use banks for such dirty work—banks that create money out of thin air in a relatively sophisticated manner (receiving permission from the state to do so, while governments and banks share the profits through other complicated and opaque mechanisms). A detailed description of these practices would likely fill many books. We don't have that much space, however, so we will simply point out the two most fundamental consequences of the actions described above: persistent inflation and economic cycles (which are the cause of economic crises). A more demanding reader can read about the principles of how business cycles arise, for instance, in the book "What Has Government Done to Our Money?" by my favorite author Murray Newton Rothbard, or "The Theory of Money and Credit" (published back in 1912!) by Ludwig von Mises, or search the internet for "Austrian business cycle theory"; a less demanding reader may perhaps be satisfied with the explanation that nothing like business cycles or persistent inflation existed until states began controlling money. I would genuinely love to explore this topic in greater depth, because the tools with which governments, aided by banks, control money are almost diabolical; however, describing them in detail would take another separate book. Let us now turn instead to something that fills me with hope—namely, cryptomoney.

chapter: 5. Money
name: Cryptomoney
text:
In 2013, when the Money chapter was written, the fundamental significance of cryptomoney was not yet entirely clear to me, which is why I did not include it then; however, I would consider it a major omission not to mention it now in the second edition. Cryptomoney is digital money whose existence and transfers are secured through cryptography by decentralized networks rather than central authorities; this means it needs no central bank, while still providing all the advantages of online means of payment.

There is a consensus among economists that for a good to be classified as money, it must perform three basic functions: store value, serve as a universal medium of exchange, and act as a unit of account (that is, serve as a measure of prices of goods and services in the economy); I personally believe that nothing can be a unit of account unless it is also a universal medium of exchange, so the second function described is redundant, as it follows directly from the third. History shows that these functions are performed by commodities possessing the following six properties: scarcity (limited supply), durability, fungibility (ideally, the indistinguishability of units of the given item), divisibility (the ability to subdivide into smaller units without loss of value), easy portability, and recognizability (verification of authenticity). Not everything that possesses these attributes automatically becomes money; good money, however, must satisfy all of these parameters (at least to a considerable degree).

All six criteria are met very well by a number of goods commonly called cryptocurrencies; some of them serve as great stores of value, though none is yet widely used as a universal medium of exchange, and thus not as a unit of account either. State (fiat) currencies meet most of these six criteria far worse, yet their acceptance is enforced by law (moreover, there is an obligation to pay taxes and keep accounts in them); as a result, they function as units of account and media of exchange, yet fail as stores of value (since nothing guarantees their scarcity when banks continually issue new ones). Thus, neither any cryptocurrency (due to insufficient liquidity) nor fiat (due to a steady decline in real purchasing power) fulfills all the functions of good money today. For cryptocurrencies capable of storing value over the long term, I prefer the term cryptomoney, thereby distinguishing them from liquid—yet relentlessly depreciating—state currencies, as well as from the vast majority (over 99.99%) of cryptocurrencies, which are referred to in the crypto community by the established term "shitcoins."

The oldest, most widespread, most liquid, and for many (so-called Bitcoin maximalists) the only cryptomoney is Bitcoin. This protocol for an open-source peer-to-peer payment network was defined in late 2008 by a person or group of people operating under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto; on January 3, 2009, it was launched, initially serving as a toy for a few enthusiasts. A year and a half later, someone used it for a purchase for the first time—programmer Laszlo Hanyecz ordered two pizzas for 10,000 BTC; little did he suspect back then that in honor of this transaction, crypto-anarchists would begin celebrating May 22 as "Pizza Day" a few years later. Today, for the same number of bitcoins, we could buy, say, a large private island with a luxury palace, power plant, airport, harbor, private jet, helicopter, yacht, and maybe even a submarine; and we wouldn't have to worry much about the budget—there would be plenty left over for operating costs for the rest of our lives. How could the price rise so much? More and more people are realizing that Bitcoin is an outstanding store of value—far better than any current fiat currency.

From the perspective of a (crypto)anarchist, I view the absence of any central authority as Bitcoin's most important feature; it is a decentralized network that anyone can join at any time and begin participating in its operation. While balance records in ordinary bank accounts are managed by banks (which can therefore freeze them and the like), all Bitcoin transactions (including its complete history) are stored simultaneously by tens of thousands of computers distributed around the world; and if one happens to decide to block my funds, another will simply process my transfer request. Cynics claim that the intelligence services of some major power might be hiding behind the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto, which I do not consider very likely; the beauty of decentralization, however, lies above all in the fact that it is completely irrelevant—even if it were true, Bitcoin's creator has no actual power over it (nor even a backdoor, since it is open-source software with publicly accessible source code).

Conversely, I consider Bitcoin's greatest weakness to be that it is not fully anonymous; while it does not show who owns which funds, their transfers can be traced—the history of all transactions is public (although they cannot be linked to specific individuals without additional information, states are gradually devoting more and more resources to obtaining that "additional information"). While this problem can be solved in most cases to protect one's privacy, doing so requires an advanced understanding of how the entire network operates as well as blockchain-analysis tools—not to mention that anyone can simply make mistakes, as a result of which, unfortunately, a number of seasoned crypto-anarchists have gotten to see the inside of a prison cell. In response to this, projects such as Monero emerged—one can picture it as Bitcoin's "younger brother," except that it operates in complete anonymity and nobody can track others' transactions without the author's permission; that is also why it is commonly used on illegal darknet markets (though it has other limitations of its own). For completeness, let me note that Bitcoin has tens of thousands of different "siblings"; almost without exception, however, these are broken or outright fraudulent projects (the aforementioned "shitcoins") in which you can easily lose your savings—yet their existence provides much-needed competition that separates the wheat from the chaff (and I still consider some of them more trustworthy than state currencies).

As I mentioned a few paragraphs ago, no cryptomoney yet performs all the necessary functions of (good) money; and given the inflationary nature of absolutely all fiat currencies, I dare say that unfortunately no good money exists in the world today. The six properties that form a necessary (though not sufficient) prerequisite for a commodity to become such money are, in my opinion, currently best fulfilled by Bitcoin and Monero. Let us make a brief comparison of these cryptomonies, precious metals, and state currencies:

Scarcity

Bitcoin: Excellent - fixed maximum number of coins

Monero: Very good - low, predictable inflation

Precious metals: Good - potential new deposits

State fiat currencies: Poor - unpredictable central-bank inflation

Durability

Bitcoin: Excellent - distributed database

Monero: Excellent - distributed database

Precious metals: Excellent - tangible physical goods

State fiat currencies: Good - central control over account balances

Fungibility

Bitcoin: Poor - public coin history

Monero: Excellent - coins invisible without keys

Precious metals: Excellent - indistinguishable coins and bullion

State fiat currencies: Very good - digital trail of cashless transactions

Divisibility

Bitcoin: Excellent - easily divisible "to dust"

Monero: Excellent - easily divisible "to dust"

Precious metals: Very good - divisible almost "to dust"

State fiat currencies: Very good - easily broken into smaller units

Portability

Bitcoin: Excellent - keys portable in your head

Monero: Excellent - keys portable in your head

Precious metals: Good - tangible physical goods

State fiat currencies: Very good - physical cash, bank-controlled accounts

Recognizability

Bitcoin: Excellent - public blockchain

Monero: Very good - complex cryptographic verifiability

Precious metals: Good - chemical testability

State fiat currencies: Good - anti-counterfeiting features on banknotes and coins

I consider it important to add that not all properties are equally important; for example, poor recognizability of money need not be such a major obstacle (say, if the commodities it can be exchanged for are also scarce), whereas minimal scarcity or an extremely short lifespan of a good essentially makes its monetary use impossible. Furthermore, it is not true that the item best meeting the above parameters must always become money; switching currencies entails high transaction costs, which is why people only abandon their existing money when it stops performing the necessary functions—not merely because something else might perform them slightly better. For instance, Bitcoin has (and has always had) the highest market capitalization (i.e., the product of the number of bitcoins and the current unit price) of all cryptomonies; it serves as a good store of value that can be transferred quickly and cheaply between individual holders across virtually any distance. Even though other cryptomonies (such as Monero) later introduced certain advantages (such as anonymity), for most users the time-tested trustworthiness of the first and oldest open-source peer-to-peer payment network clearly matters more; for that reason (at least so far), it does not appear likely that Bitcoin will lose its "number one" position (at least in the foreseeable future).

If (any) money ceases to be scarce, its value declines, which can go so far that people refuse to accept and use it as a universal medium of exchange; in the case of state currencies, this fate can to some extent be delayed (or even averted) by legislation—for example, by mandating their acceptance by merchants or prohibiting the payment of taxes (or keeping of accounts) in any other medium. Naturally, not even these measures are a silver bullet; during hyperinflation, for instance, alternatives to the debased money typically enter the scene. Until the situation becomes untenable, however, the state successfully enforces the use of bad money by force, thereby harming its holders; inflation (of virtually all current fiat currencies) represents a hidden form of taxation.

It will probably surprise no one that as a (crypto)anarchist I prefer cryptomoney over state money; above all, however, I am an advocate of full voluntariness, freedom of choice, and hence a free market in money—which I consider far more important than my personal preference for Bitcoin (or Monero). I believe the only way to discover truly good money is to let people choose for themselves what suits them. Even if it were somehow to turn out that centrally controlled inflationary currencies are the most desired (which I consider extremely unlikely), I will humbly accept that choice, provided it is not conditioned by violent coercion; however much I regard Bitcoin as the money of the future for many reasons, I wish to impose nothing on anyone—let everyone decide for themselves what they wish (or do not wish) to pay with.

If you know nothing at all about cryptomoney and would like to change that, you can visit the website krypto.urza.cz.

name: 6. Firefighters
text:
Private firefighters. An absence of state firefighters. When someone says something like that in mainstream society, reactions vary—mostly they are highly emotional, and we quickly arrive at vivid images of burning houses from which paying customers are rescued while everyone else perishes in the flames, jumping out of windows like human torches. Because those emotions are precisely what the state uses to manipulate its citizens, let us try to set them aside for a moment and think things through more deeply.

Since in this chapter we will discuss the manner and quality of firefighting services, it should be noted at the outset that this quality depends heavily on price; generally speaking, in almost any situation, spending extra money makes it possible to achieve higher quality. One extreme corresponds to firefighting services not being provided by anyone in any way, so that total costs equal zero. The other theoretical extreme might look roughly like having a fully equipped fire station next to every house. Between these extremes lie many intermediate states, corresponding to networks of varying density and variously equipped stations. Clearly, adding money to such a system can raise quality—for instance, by purchasing better equipment, reducing response times, and the like.

Common sense, Ludwig von Mises's remarkable book "Human Action", everyday observation, and the first two chapters of this book indicate that people have needs, which they satisfy in order from the most urgent to the least urgent (resources are scarce, so they cannot satisfy them all). In practice, this means a person typically knows they need to eat, have housing, and get to work, so those are the things they obtain first (they first use their money to pay for food, housing, and commuting); next, say, they know they would like to go to a concert and have a couple of dinners at a nice restaurant (they pay for these with what money remains); then, perhaps, they know they want to go to the seaside in the summer and buy a car in a year (from the money left after food, housing, commuting, the concert, and dinners, they set some aside as savings); and finally, they might also like to go to the movies, only to find they have no money left for it—meaning they skip the movies because their other needs are more important. Every one of us thinks roughly along these lines: we rank our needs and desires and satisfy the most urgent, greatest ones. Some might object that there are also people who do not plan things out so deliberately and act more impulsively, or are too lazy to think about it and make sensible calculations; in short, one can answer such objections by noting that for those people, impulsiveness or laziness (whose expressions are in a sense also needs) takes precedence over satisfying some of the needs listed above (for anyone who finds this answer insufficient, I refer them to the aforementioned book "Human Action", in which Ludwig von Mises describes such behavior in great detail).

How does this relate to firefighters? Well, fire protection is among the needs of the vast majority of people, and everyone feels this need to a different degree. Some are willing to pay a great deal for very high-quality service, while others would rather pay little for an inferior service. What happens when the state sets a fixed level of service quality? Those for whom that quality is insufficient will typically buy something better; indeed, many industrial enterprises and high-value properties today are protected against fire by private firefighting firms (yet the owners of those protected properties are still forced, completely immorally and nonsensically, to pay for state fire protection as well). On the other hand, there are also those among us for whom state fire brigades are too costly and who would be satisfied with a cheaper—albeit worse—option. These people are violently forced to pay for something they do not want. The state simply takes one of their less urgent needs and forces them to satisfy it at the expense of a more urgent need, for which the person may then no longer have sufficient resources.

This (along with the obvious fact that forcing someone by violence to pay for any service is profoundly immoral) constitutes the main—and quite fundamental—arguments against the existence of state firefighters. Suppose, then, that we allow firefighting services to be provided purely by the free market without state intervention; what might such a system look like? Given that market solutions to problems are the outcome of interactions among vast numbers of free individuals, one cannot simply declare from an armchair exactly how it will work, though much can be estimated. I will therefore sketch one possible way the free market could provide firefighting services—and reality would likely be even better, as millions of entrepreneurs around the world would surely devise far more efficient solutions.

Judging by how private fire brigades have operated both historically and today, we can assume that payments for these services would work much like insurance. Entrepreneurs would establish fire stations in various locations, and nearby residents would pay for their services via a flat-rate subscription: each month they would pay a small fee regardless of whether a fire actually breaks out on their property; when a fire does occur, the company responds. It is reasonable to expect that entire buildings would be insured in this way (rather than individuals, who are virtually impossible to identify in time during a fire), which eliminates scenarios in which firefighters pull paying customers out of a burning building and leave the rest to burn (insurance would presumably cover the entire building and everyone inside—a firefighting firm that protected property while letting people burn to death would hardly have many customers).

Another huge advantage of this arrangement is that the price of fire protection would be set individually—higher for buildings with a higher probability of fire and lower for those with a lower probability. Just as today the location of a house affects the price of flood insurance (it is more expensive in floodplains), for buildings better safeguarded against fire the fire-protection fee would be lower. When these services are provided by the state and their price is independent of fire risk, there have to be mountains of fire regulations that nobody has much incentive to follow (and builders have little reason to do more than the bare minimum). If the price of fire protection is market-based, following (and developing) "fire codes" becomes economically advantageous both for those who construct buildings and for those who maintain and live in them. Nobody will have to force anyone to do anything; people will be motivated simply by saving money when they follow certain rules.

Suppose some people do not take out fire insurance. It is very likely that companies providing firefighting services on a regular subscription basis would also be willing to put out a fire for a direct one-off fee, which would logically be much higher than the regular insurance premium; in any case, since we are talking about saving a house, it practically always pays for the owner to pay such a fee, because the value of the house is typically higher than the cost of extinguishing the fire. Nor can one argue that the poor would be unable to afford fire protection: anyone who owns a house or an apartment also has the means to pay firefighters; even if they chose not to pay regular fees, in the event of a fire they can still call a firm to extinguish the property—it will be worth their while at practically any price lower than the value of whatever remains of the property after the fire is put out.

Other free-market options include, for example, company fire brigades (a factory maintains its own brigade, which also fights fires in the surrounding area) or volunteer firefighters (a role that carries social prestige); in Austria, for instance, these cover a significantly larger share of the market than state brigades, while in Denmark most fires are extinguished by commercial firms. Historically, too, private fire brigades have proved their worth. State-funded fire departments are a relatively modern phenomenon; for the most part, they did not begin appearing until the late nineteenth century, and even then they covered nowhere near as large a share of the market as they do today (that came only in the twentieth century). Previously, firefighting services were provided and paid for in quite diverse

ways. In London, for example, the first professional fire brigades were founded back in the seventeenth century; they were funded by insurance companies and were highly successful—in a city built almost entirely of wood, they responded several times a day and extinguished hundreds of thousands of fires (anyone interested in the details can find them, for instance, in "An Economic History of London 1800–1914" by Michael Ball and David Sunderland). On the territory of today's Czech Republic, fire brigades were mostly volunteer-based and funded through charity, or else factory fire associations (whose primary task was to put out fires at factories, though they typically protected the surrounding neighborhood as well); the funds for their operation were sufficient even without state intervention (more details can be found, for example, in Josef Bartoš's "History of Moravia, Vol. 4: Free State and Occupation").

Market prices will also ensure appropriate wages for firefighters (what they deserve—that is, what people are willing to pay them voluntarily) as well as the "right" number of them. Everyone has surely heard some politician declare that they will halt cuts to fire-brigade staffing or ensure an increase in their numbers; we constantly hear that there are too few state employees and that they cannot perform their work to the required extent. Conversely, how often do we hear calls for centrally mandated increases in the headcount of bakers, programmers, laborers, or shop clerks? Nothing of the sort is needed, because the invisible hand of the market can ensure the right number of them (when there are too few people in a given profession, their wages rise, attracting more people to train for it, and vice versa—these principles are described in more detail in the first two chapters of this book). It would be exactly the same with firefighters—if only the state stopped regulating this sector and left room for the free market.

Although fire protection is generally perceived as a good that ought to be provided by the state because "otherwise it wouldn't work," upon closer inspection we find that it worked long ago and still works today in some countries; moreover, there is really no reason why it shouldn't work. On the contrary, there are many arguments showing why private firefighting services are not only more moral (nobody forces anyone by violence to pay for them), but also more efficient. Unfortunately, we are given no choice—the state forces us through violence to pay for its services; the same can be said of subsidizing culture, to which we will devote more attention in the very next chapter.

name: 7. Art and Culture
text:
Culture—and art in general—enriches a person in spirit and mind and benefits society; therefore, it ought to be supported by state subsidies, lest many beautiful things vanish from our world. Some art pays for itself, while other art would perish without subsidies—and surely we must protect the latter from extinction. That is roughly what most people say when asked what they think about state funding of culture. Let us think more deeply about the consequences, however, before jumping to any hasty conclusion.

At the outset, I want to make clear that I am certainly no "enemy of art." People often tend to assume that anyone who condemns cultural subsidies is against art as such. That need not be true, and in my case it is definitely false. I consider both art and culture very important, for they truly enrich individuals and make them happy—in my own case, for example, especially rock and classical music.

Defenders of cultural subsidies from public budgets justify their position mainly by claiming that without subsidies many artists could not create, theaters would disappear, "non-commercial" cinema could not sustain itself, and exhibitions and museums could not cover their costs from admission fees alone. To begin addressing this objection, it must be noted that many great artists created without state support; to name just a few across various art forms: Shakespeare, G. B. Shaw, Beethoven, Mozart (who, in his eccentricity, refused to serve powerful patrons and became an independent artist), Queen, Pink Floyd, Deep Purple, The Rolling Stones, Leonardo da Vinci, Raphael, Vincent van Gogh, Picasso, Dalí...

Above all, however, we must realize what it actually means when, without state subsidies, an artist cannot create, a theater closes down, a film cannot be made, or a museum cannot cover its operating costs. When such art cannot sustain itself, it is because people are unwilling to pay enough for it voluntarily (without state coercion), meaning the costs of producing that art exceed what people are willing to pay for the outcome. From the first chapter, however, we know that such a situation means someone is wasting scarce resources (such as the artist's time, the theater building, canvas and paint, or musical instruments); people value those resources as worth more than what was created from them (if that were not the case, the art in question would be profitable). This means that the net utility of such an artistic endeavor for people is negative.

I can picture readers indignantly objecting at this point that art and beauty surely cannot be reduced to mere money! Please recall the opening chapters of this book. What is the main function of money and prices? Precisely to convey information about the scarcity of goods and the utility people derive from them. Translating something into "mere" money simultaneously means translating it into human utility and satisfaction. Obviously, the mere fact that more money would have to be spent on a project than people are willing to pay for it afterward is not what matters on its own. What matters is what this information tells us: people do not want that project. We must keep opportunity costs in mind—alongside whatever benefit the project yields, we must also factor in that other things could not be created because of it; the people involved could have been doing something else, and the materials could have been used differently. Even the value of those people's time and the materials used exceeds the value of the resulting work (and while that value is numerically expressed in money, what it fundamentally represents is utility for society).

Most people live under the impression that the "value of art" is something only experts or critics can determine, because many ordinary people "don't understand art." Yet what is the actual purpose of art or culture? Surely its purpose is to enrich a person in spirit, heart, and mind, to make them happier, to evoke pleasant feelings, to prompt reflection. But what kind of person? Everyone! Not merely a handful of initiates. Those who "don't understand art" are not enriched by it. Yet they are no less human than those who do understand; their wishes, desires, feelings, and dreams are no less important—and it is therefore monstrous to force them to pay for something they have no interest in. I am not claiming that "quality art" is whatever pays for itself; I simply do not want to force anyone through violence to pay for it.

One often encounters the objection that if the state did not support art, only "commercial" stuff and "trash" would survive, whereas truly "valuable" works would not—that mindless TV series or monotonous pop music would sustain themselves, for instance, while genuinely deeper works would struggle to survive. Yet what does that mean? It means that the monotonous pop music and mindless TV series that pay for themselves make people happier than the works that cannot survive without state subsidies! The objection that this is only because "they're uneducated barbarians" may be true, yet it is irrelevant—why should the happiness of a "cultured person" take precedence over the happiness of an "uneducated barbarian"? I too cannot fathom how anyone can prefer, say, Michal David to Brian May, Freddie Mercury, Beethoven, or Vivaldi; it seems completely crazy to me. Nevertheless, such people exist. And nothing gives me any right to forcibly compel them to pay for what I like at the expense of what they like. If the soap opera "Ordinace v růžové zahradě" (Rose Garden Clinic) makes someone happy, it is immoral, unethical, monstrous, and inexcusable to force them through violence to pay for the series "Italian Classics of the Second Half of the 20th Century," which they do not watch and get nothing out of—regardless of what I think of their taste (I leave it to the reader to ponder who is the greater barbarian: the person peacefully watching their favorite soap opera, or the one forcibly compelling them to subsidize his favorite theater).

Moreover, the choice is not always framed the way it is presented to us—and the way I just framed it in the previous paragraph. People who do not pay for theater or museums do not automatically spend that money on some "lowbrow trash." Often they do not spend it on any form of art at all, but instead use it to buy a home, education for their children, food, or donate it to charity. And even if cultural experts could decide (on everyone else's behalf) which art is mere junk and which is lofty enough to "deserve" government subsidies, surely nobody can seriously believe there could exist an expert on everything who could decide for others whether theater or food is more beneficial to them, or whether a painting exhibition or a charitable drive brings greater utility.

If anyone worries that art would cease to exist without government subsidies, they can rest easy. Art has always existed; this human need is far older than any state. Artists have created throughout all of history regardless of whether they had to support themselves or were backed by a private patron or a government. There is no reason to believe that right now, of all times, culture needs the state in order to exist. After all, governments take the money to subsidize culture from citizens' pockets; if they didn't, people would have more money with which they could buy, say, a more expensive theater ticket (or other art, or anything else—simply whatever brings them the greatest utility). Not to mention that according to the Czech Statistical Office (a 2011 study), even today the state accounts for less than fourteen percent of cultural funding; the remaining eighty-six percent was paid voluntarily.

In addition to subsidizing contemporary artists and cultural institutions, governments often look after the preservation of older works of art and historical monuments. Why will the free market handle this too to people's greater satisfaction? When works of art are no longer managed by the state, that role falls to their owners. Who will those owners be? Over time, the free market ensures they will be the people willing to pay the most for the item in question—those for whom it holds the greatest value; such owners can also be expected to take care of the artwork (or historical monument) when they have paid dearly for it. And these owners need not only be wealthy individuals; they can also be voluntary associations of many people who share the same interest and are willing to pool their money for it.

Common objections to abolishing state oversight of artworks or monuments run roughly like this: "What if someone bought St. Vitus Cathedral and opened a supermarket inside?" "Who will stop someone from buying the Mona Lisa and destroying it?" The answer is obvious: why would someone pay a fortune for a painting only to destroy it? The case of a supermarket in St. Vitus Cathedral is similar: if someone wants to run a supermarket in central Prague, why would they pay an enormous sum for a cathedral—which many others value far more highly for different purposes—when they can buy another building in a similarly prime location for much less? Even if someone already owned the cathedral and wanted to open a supermarket, it would pay for him to sell it as a cathedral and use the proceeds to buy a cheaper building (pocketing the difference). One can naturally object that none of the above represents a 100% guarantee, yet the state gives us no such guarantee either; we need not look far for an example—just recall how many works of art and historical monuments were damaged or destroyed by the state on the territory of the Czech Republic between 1948 and 1989.

Many also object that if works of art and historical monuments are owned by the wealthy, the general public will not be able to enjoy them. First, that need not be true, because private owners too can display their property (whether free of charge or for an admission fee) or lend it out to various exhibitions (which they have always done to varying degrees and still do today). But if an owner is unwilling to do anything of the sort, people can always band together and raise a sum large enough to buy the artwork or historical monument from him. If they fail to raise such an amount voluntarily, it means the current owner values the item more than the general public, which then obviously has no right to take it from him by force.

When reflecting on government subsidies for culture, we must never forget that no matter how wonderful the art that might not (or might) pay for itself, state subsidies always mean forcibly taking money from people who wish to use it otherwise (if they didn't, they would fund that art voluntarily). Works that people are unwilling to pay for themselves voluntarily bring them less utility than the money they cost. If culture is left to the free market, only art that gives people more than it takes from them will come into being—something nobody else can decide for them except themselves.

name: 8. Education
text:
Schooling and the educational system have—at least in our part of the world—been inextricably tied to the state for over two hundred years. Today, this means that the "rules of the game" in education are set by the government, which decides what must be taught, how it may be taught, who is allowed to teach it, who is allowed to learn it, who is forced to learn it, for how long they must be taught, how they must be evaluated, and what punishment awaits anyone who defies any of these mandates. And it is especially for readers who do not already find those reasons alone sufficient for abolishing state education that this chapter was written.

The Achilles' heel of our state education system is... our state education system. Practically nothing in it works well (save for a handful of individual schools). Critical thinking is punished, individuality is suppressed, students' attitude toward authority is warped, memorization of completely useless information is demanded, graduates of many schools lack useful knowledge, students grow ever more brazen toward teachers, some teachers bully students, teachers' salaries are low, many terrible teachers just slack off in schools and are overpaid for doing nothing, and students have no interest in the lessons.

Does it strike you that solutions to some of the problems listed above might contradict one another? Your impression is quite right. Isn't such a critique of state education unfair, then, when it seems to demand one thing and at the same time its opposite? Not at all; on the contrary, it accurately points to the first fundamental problem of state education—one that the free market can solve: in state education, uniform rules apply that may differ in minor details, yet their basic direction is centrally determined in a uniform manner (see the "National Education Program"). Nothing of the sort exists on the free market. Every school can teach whatever its customers want.

Not all parents share the same vision for raising their children. For some, religious upbringing (and there are many religions) and, say, sexual abstinence are important; others want to shield their children from religion and favor today's modern approach to sex education. For some, conformity, discipline, obedience, and submission to authority matter most; others emphasize individuality, independent judgment, questioning the reasons behind rules rather than following them automatically, and following only authorities whom their children choose for themselves. Some of us prefer "amikace" (anti-manipulative education) over traditional upbringing. Countless approaches exist; and since we are not all alike, one cannot even objectively claim that any single one is universally best for everyone. And why search for compromises or golden means when different schools can exist with different rules and different curricula? That is something the free market, by its very nature, will offer incomparably better than the state, which simply cannot provide such variety to the required degree (due to the impossibility of economic calculation—see Mises's book "Bureaucracy", or, in brief, the second chapter of this book).

Another unsolvable problem of state education is the fact that there is—and can be—no way within it to distinguish a good teacher from a bad one. Practically anyone who obtains the requisite diploma can go teach. The government then oversees (and poorly at that) only whether a teacher is so egregiously bad that it becomes obvious (such as showing up drunk to work). Aside from such extreme cases, the state simply has no ability to differentiate teachers by quality. And given that a teacher's quality cannot be measured precisely—and different teachers are good or bad for different students—this task is impossible for central planners. The market solves this problem completely automatically, just as in any other industry: the better someone is at what they do, the more people are willing to pay for their services. No central algorithm is needed to determine the quality of architects, programmers, graphic designers, or chefs (a good chef wins customers for his restaurant, and vice versa). The exact same would hold for teachers on the free market.

The logical consequence of the inability to evaluate teacher quality is rigid pay scales. And what happens when an employee receives the same pay for work done well and work done poorly? It is obvious at first glance that this encourages everyone to slack off. Moreover, another consequence must be recognized: for capable specialists, teaching is a miserably paid job, because they can earn more elsewhere; conversely, for good-for-nothings who can barely scrape together a degree from some lousy teachers' college, such a job is wonderfully paid, since nobody else would pay them more. Unfortunately, it follows that the more capable a person is in a given field, the less incentive state education gives them to teach (and vice versa).

A fairly typical objection to free-market education is that some poor (or stingy, or education-blind) parents supposedly wouldn't pay for their children's schooling, which could leave some—perhaps talented—children without an education. Well, if a child is truly capable, it pays for schools to teach them for free (or very cheaply), because such students raise the school's standard (both by "pulling" less talented classmates upward and by improving the school's statistics of successful graduates) and provide great advertising (this is no idle theory—it already happens at many private schools today). Additional solutions are offered by homeschooling or community education, charity, or company-sponsored schools whose graduates can subsequently become employees (which can even be stipulated by contract).

Naturally, these solutions require at least minimal cooperation from parents, which at first glance may look like a drawback; upon closer reflection, however, it is clear that when a parent is an ignoramus who simply doesn't care about their child, the state doesn't help much anyway (it usually manages to get the child into school, yet the school typically gives that student practically nothing; he, in turn, often disrupts class and "enriches" his classmates with things their parents—and teachers—would rather do without). If someone now objects that even a slight increase in the odds of a good life for a "problem child" is worth a try, I ask them: "Are the odds for problem children so important to you that you wouldn't mind having your own children be their classmates—and not infrequently targets of bullying?" Because someone's children will have to be. Besides, by "giving chances to problem children" and placing them in an environment where everyone constantly makes them feel inadequate, the state may very well end up doing them more harm than good as well (see the fourth chapter).

A common objection to leaving education to the free market goes something like this: "After all, we already have private schools now—just look at them, most of them are worthless and often just sell diplomas." Here it must be noted that even though a school is privately owned, the state dictates what it may not, may, and must do, ergo it has practically nothing in common with the free market (to say nothing of artificial competition in the form of state schools). In such an environment, it really can be profitable simply to teach poorly and hand out diplomas. On a free market, however, the value of a diploma would correspond to the reputation of the school in question (and if anyone could obtain it easily, it would become worthless—just as today the value of certificates from training courses is determined precisely by their quality); furthermore, one can assume there would be independent certification firms evaluating students' knowledge regardless of which school they attended. The incentive for such certification authorities to do their job well is clear: if they certified everyone (say, for a fee), their certifications would lose all value, and demand for their services would vanish.
