Yet the main advantage of the free market—one that today's private schools operating under the state's baton lack—is the freedom to choose to teach in one's own way. That is the core strength of the free market! Millions of people start schools and try out all kinds of teaching methods; the good ones prosper, the bad ones go bankrupt. The state has no room for anything like that: first, it cannot test countless possibilities simultaneously, and second, it cannot afford much experimentation.

Throughout this chapter, I have been emphasizing that the state allows schools to teach essentially in only one way and restricts them far too much. Yet our laws do allow schools to specialize in different fields, within which they can have significantly different hour allocations for individual subjects—so what's the problem? Such reasoning shows that we have unfortunately become so conditioned by the practice of state education that we cannot imagine anything else. With a bit of imagination, however, we might ask ourselves questions like these: Is it necessary for any subjects to be taught in school at all? Must students be graded or evaluated (in any way)? Is age segregation into grade levels necessary? Must teachers motivate children to learn? Even if we think we have the answers to these—and all other—questions, how can we know for sure until someone tries?

There is even an educational theory describing a school that would operate roughly like this: students would not be segregated by age in any way; there would be no grade levels, even though the planned age range is quite wide (roughly from four to nineteen years old). No subjects would be taught at the school. Students would have tools and resources (computers, a playground, a library, workshops, learning supplies, notebooks, stationery, a garden...) at their free disposal. Nobody would even force them to learn to read and write. There would be no grades, no oral exams, no tests. Teachers would not issue top-down directives; they would simply help when asked by the children. The initiative, however, must always come from the student—nobody is allowed to force anyone to do anything. All essential school matters that cannot be decided individually and require a collective decision are settled by simple majority vote, where students' and teachers' votes carry equal weight—so the vote of a four-year-old counts the same as the vote of a nineteen-year-old, which in turn counts the same as the vote of a teacher. Such voting would include, for example, deciding which teachers receive a contract for the following year.

Would you choose such a school for your children? I would. If there were more of us, perhaps the market would show that this system of education makes sense. However, nobody would have to participate in this experiment against their will. There is nothing wrong with someone having a different idea about raising their children. On the free market, countless different solutions can be implemented simultaneously, because it is not bound by any central planning on the part of the state.

chapter: 8. Education
name: Education and freedom
text:
I ended the previous—that is, the eighth—chapter by introducing an unconventional and very free educational model that illustrates another way a school could look. Does it strike you as unrealistic? Did you find yourself thinking I couldn't possibly be serious about this anymore? Is it merely an armchair theory with no basis in practice? A concept that could never work with real children?

When I first read about this educational model, roughly those same thoughts ran through my head. Whenever I discussed the topic with an educator, the reactions were almost always negative. It is precisely one of those teaching methods that no government would ever dare introduce, because it contradicts everything we know about education—so, of course, it could never work.

Yet Hanna and Daniel Greenberg thought otherwise. In 1968, they decided to found just such a school: the Sudbury Valley School, where there are no lessons, no subjects are taught, no one forces students to do anything, gives them grades, or evaluates them in any other way; they are simply given the space to do whatever they want. There are no classes, and children are not segregated by age; on the contrary, everyone is kept together—from four-year-olds to nineteen-year-olds. Decision-making (including which teachers will or will not have their contracts renewed) is handled by voting, in which everyone's vote—four-year-olds, nineteen-year-olds, and teachers alike—carries equal weight.

The results? Excellent. Over its fifty years of existence, the Sudbury Valley School has produced hundreds of successful graduates who, among other things—surprisingly—are able to transition into conventional state education: eighty percent of them have earned a university degree. In all those years, there has not been a single graduate of this school who could not read and write (even though that is a very common objection raised by opponents of this style of education). Bullying is also nonexistent at Sudbury Valley. Psychologists who have studied this phenomenon explain it in two ways. First, they believe the absence of age segregation plays a major role, as weaker children (frequent victims of bullying) are not forced to measure themselves against same-age peers and can spend time with younger kids (moreover, older students often stand up for younger ones). Second, they believe children tend to adopt the behavioral patterns they see around them. That is why bullying flourishes in schools where teachers treat students in an authoritarian manner (the same can be observed on a harsher scale during military service), whereas it does not occur at Sudbury Valley, where no one encounters such behavior. You can read more about this school in the publications of psychologist Peter Gray, or simply search the internet for "Sudbury Valley."

Although Sudbury Valley is probably the most popular and well-known of the free schools, it is neither the only one nor the first. The oldest known similar project in modern history was launched by the anarchist Francisco Ferrer Guardia in 1901 in Barcelona; five years later, however, he was arrested for allegedly collaborating in another anarchist's attempt to assassinate the king. Although the state never proved this charge, it imprisoned him for over a year anyway, during which time his school collapsed. The first still-operating (and extraordinarily successful) educational institution of this type was founded by Alexander Sutherland Neill in 1921 in Germany, from where it moved to Austria, and since 1923 it has been based in England.

The successes of these schools have inspired many other enthusiasts and entrepreneurs; dozens of similar institutions have been founded in several countries around the world. Their results are very similar to those I described above for Sudbury Valley. Despite these demonstrable and fascinating successes, the legislation of many states rejects such schools. This means that if someone were to open such an institution here in the Czech Republic, for example, the state would not recognize it as a school; consequently, attending it would not count toward compulsory school attendance, and the students' parents would get into trouble with child protective services as if they were neglecting their children. Makes sense, doesn't it?

I consider it important to emphasize that I am definitely not claiming that all education should look like this or that all schools should operate on the Sudbury model. I assume that for some children this method of education is suitable, and for others it is not (after all, the same can be said of any system, including the current one). That does not mean, however, that it should be banned across the board. People are different; why, then, suppress their individuality and try to indoctrinate them under the threat of violence, doing everything possible to force their education into a single uniform mold created by the state?

As long as the government sets the rules for the entire education system, however, many good ways of educating will never have a chance to emerge. When someone comes up with rules for a school like the one at Sudbury Valley, the vast majority of people (especially educators and all sorts of education experts) say it could never work. So no one tries it, and the concept remains mere theory. And of course, this is not just about the Sudbury model! There are countless theoretical approaches to education, and the only way to find out which ones work in practice is for someone to simply step up and try them (while, naturally, no one would force any parents to send their children to such a school—that would be entirely up to them). Yet as long as people are not free to experiment in this way, they cannot try, and many good educational models remain only on paper.

Unfortunately, one of the reasons most states have taken such complete control over schooling and the education system is precisely to ensure that every individual is properly indoctrinated and thoroughly taught from childhood that it is morally justifiable and justified for some people to rule over others—that he is merely a citizen who needs a ruler, and should consider himself lucky that he at least gets to vote for one. Don't believe me? Pick up any textbook on social studies or civics (even the very name of the subject implies training for citizenship). Still don't believe me? Just read the "National Education Program," where you will find references to (I quote) education for democratic citizenship, strengthening a sense of belonging [...] to national traditions, key competencies aimed especially at [...] educating the citizen, and introducing elements of democracy into school life. I completely understand and respect that some readers may consider this right, but do not force me to expose my children to it.

I have discussed the Sudbury model with many people—often with teachers, and even with two education experts who have devoted their entire careers to teaching, teaching others how to teach, publishing textbooks, and doing various work for the Ministry of Education. I always began by describing the model as a theory and discussing it purely hypothetically; the people I spoke with had no idea that such schools actually exist. Most often, I got roughly this response (and the more experience in pedagogy the person had, the more categorically and confidently they delivered it): "That is a lovely theory that sounds very nice, but it could never work in practice. I know what I'm talking about—students simply behave differently." Of course they behave differently! How could they not, when they are educated in a completely different environment? The problem with every such educator (or education expert) is precisely that they judge everything solely by what they see in current schooling. Yet it is unreasonable to assume that because students behave a certain way in one educational model, they will behave the same way in a diametrically different one.

This brings to mind a parallel regarding how society functions. In discussions about a stateless society, many people very often assume that people in such a society would behave the same way they do today. That, of course, is a big mistake. People currently do not take care of certain things and do not do certain things simply because the state does them for them. It is a mistake to believe that if the state stopped taking care of those things, people would not change their behavior. That is just as short-sighted as condemning the Sudbury model on the grounds that it wouldn't work if students behaved in it the same way they do in today's schools.

Put people in shackles, and they will become aggressive and distrustful. Chain someone to a wall, and he will try to break free, acting hostile and suspicious. Then unchain him from the wall and give him slightly longer chains. What will you observe? He will become even more aggressive; seeing a chance, he will try all the harder to escape, because now he can at least do something. What do you conclude from that? That more shackles and shorter chains are needed, because a man chained to a wall is calmer than one who can at least move around the room? Yet that is precisely how many people think about the state: the more the state "loosens the chains," the worse people will supposedly behave and the more they will abuse it. But the glaring truth is the exact opposite. The solution is to release the person from his shackles and give him freedom. Because freedom is natural, he will then be content.

I can observe this in myself as well. As long as I believed in the state, obeyed its laws, and lived under the influence of propaganda, I cared more about what was written in the law than what was right. I followed laws out of principle—even when I could have benefited from breaking them; it seemed to me that a good person respects the law. When I freed myself from that mindset, two things happened. First, my mind is free—a wonderful feeling, believe me. Second, I understood that morality and ethics are superior to laws. I follow laws either when I voluntarily choose to do so, or when breaking them would bring punishment; otherwise, they mean nothing more to me than shackles I never consented to, forced upon me by a government I have no interest in and never chose. I therefore feel no obligation to respect its bonds and have no qualms about casting them off at any time. Yet that does not mean I have turned into a scoundrel. Quite the opposite. I have even found myself in situations where I could have profited simply by invoking the law, yet I chose to do what was right rather than what was legal. I no longer look at what is written, but at what is good and what is bad. And I dare say this transformation has made me a better person than I was before.

I am certainly not saying that if the state did not exist, everyone would suddenly start behaving honestly and uprightly. It is clear to me that they would not. However, I am convinced that a sizable share of people would become more responsible, because they would have to take care of themselves. And I believe that responsibility is a virtue that leads to further virtues...

chapter: 8. Education
name: Education and propaganda
text:
The Sudbury Valley School is based on just one of a vast number of different educational models; however, there are also approaches that reject schooling altogether, no matter how free it may be (so-called unschooling), and often treat complete voluntariness on the part of the learner as a necessary condition for working at all—which naturally rules out their legal use in any country with legislated compulsory schooling or compulsory education (that is, de facto everywhere). While I do not claim that every educational model is suitable for everyone, I see no reason why some of them (or, in fact, most of them) should be outlawed.

In the Czech Republic, for example, practically the only legal model of education is the so-called "Prussian cadet school" (and its variants)—that is, schools with teachers, class periods, classrooms, grades, discipline, age segregation, obedience, and compulsory attendance. Why is it sometimes called the "Prussian cadet school"? Well, long ago, the Prussian military brass complained that schools were producing poor soldiers for their needs, ones who thought too much and did not obey orders blindly enough. So a reform was carried out with the goal of reshaping schooling to produce ideal, obedient killing machines—and it is within this very model (after some relatively minor modifications) that our children are still educated today. Against that backdrop, it is amusing when teachers talk about developing students' critical thinking, independence, and the like, while trying to achieve all of this within a system designed for the exact opposite. It is rather like wanting absolute silence, going to look for it at a music festival, and wondering why tweaking the parameters of your earplugs fails to yield the desired result.

An integral part of today's education system is teachers whom students typically did not choose, yet must obey and often even show a kind of deference to (standing up when the instructor enters the classroom is a prime example). In this way, even young children are conditioned to feel that it is desirable and right to submit to an external authority they did not choose for themselves. First it is the teacher, who is eventually replaced by the government, a politician, a police officer, a bureaucrat—in short, whatever oppressor the state dreams up. Someone might object that such training is good preparation for future employment, since most people have a boss at work; however, a person chooses such a job and is there voluntarily (not that they necessarily like it there, but no one forces them to be there).

To be clear, I have no objection whatsoever to natural authority that a person chooses of their own free will and recognizes only to the extent they deem appropriate; I consider it healthy and natural to respect someone, value them, and learn from them. What is crucial, however, is that everyone chooses for themselves whom they consider worth following. Imposing authority, by contrast, leads to a loss of self-confidence and needless conformity simply because it is expected and drilled in automatically. Indeed, the difference between forcibly imposing authority and voluntarily accepting it marks the boundary between "throwing away one's self-respect and learning to bow down before anyone placed over us" and "accepting another person, respecting them, valuing them flaws and all, and wanting to learn from them." I want my children to have the healthy self-esteem and perspective to decide freely for themselves who deserves their respect, and I flatly refuse to have them forced to show deference to whomever someone else assigns to them. What about you? Do you want your children to grow up to be obedient citizens first and foremost, or good people? Do you want them to do what someone tells them, or what they believe is right?

Trying to enforce conformity by force where natural authority is lacking is not the only—and unfortunately not even the biggest—problem with state education; I consider the indoctrination of the very young with state propaganda to be at least as insidious. How would you like it if, say, a private company managed to insert promotion of its products into mandatory school lessons, not labeled as advertising, but presented as objective truth? Do you find that completely unacceptable? If so, why doesn't it bother you that the state does the exact same thing? Without any debate, it presents itself as the sole solution wherever "market failure" supposedly occurs. Sure, not everyone agrees on whether the market fails or not, yet even then it is an open question, not an established fact, as these alleged "market failures" are taught. As a result, the state's atrocities (curtailing our liberties and using aggressive violence) are excused as a necessity—and sometimes the means used to justify such conduct include outright, blatant lies.

Do you think I am exaggerating? Let me illustrate my point with the example of freedom of speech: in school we are taught that before 1989 we did not have it, whereas now we do. Yet try publicly promoting Nazism or racism, or endorsing certain criminal acts; if you are persistent enough, they will eventually arrest you and lock you up. So no, we certainly do not have freedom of speech—only the list of things we are forbidden to say in public has changed. It is true that we are less restricted now, but that is still not freedom. And the point is not at all whether we agree with such laws or not; I am merely pointing out that our proclaimed freedom of speech is nothing but a lie. Even if laws banning certain forms of expression were justified, that would not make it true that those expressions aren't banned—which contradicts the claim of freedom. Unfree speech cannot be turned into freedom simply by stopping the silencing of educated and wise people and silencing racists and neo-Nazis instead; freedom means that everyone can speak—including those whose views strike us as perverse, nonsensical, abhorrent, or stupid.

I consider the deification of the state and its symbols to be the most repulsive practice of the current educational system. Why are our children instructed, as part of compulsory schooling, to revere the flag, the national anthem, and other state symbols? That is nothing short of idolatry! If a free person decides, on the basis of life experience, to honor a particular flag or piece of music, that is of course their business, and I am the last person who would want to stop them; however, that is worlds apart from forcing a small child to sit somewhere and be manipulated into doing the same. How are people who have gone through this education system supposed to view the state impartially and critically when they have been made to worship it like an idol from early childhood? Incidentally, the same goes for democracy, which is uncritically presented as an inherent good in much the same way; notice how often the word "undemocratic" is used as a synonym for "bad" (even in reference to entirely democratic processes).

It is impossible for such heavy propaganda at the most impressionable age not to leave a lasting mark on people; everyone then "knows" that a society without a state cannot function without ever having seriously thought about it. When you introduce someone to the idea of a stateless society for the first time, in the vast majority of cases a dismissive reaction arrives within seconds. I cannot help wondering how anyone can take a firm stand in a matter of seconds on an issue so complex that genuinely thinking it through requires tens or hundreds of hours. Unfortunately, there is only one way: the person must have "known" it already in advance, without ever subjecting the idea to critical thinking or engaging with the arguments. Sadly, whenever we "know" something without having arrived at that "knowledge" through any reasoned process, we simply reject logical arguments; we hear them, yet automatically dismiss them as mistaken without even admitting the possibility that they might be true.

Unfortunately, this applies not only to discussions about the state, but to many other topics as well—and none of us are immune. The only way to fight it is through a constant, lifelong effort to recognize all the places where we accept various dogmas without critical evaluation. When I first uncovered several such instances in myself, I was pleased to think I had "finally gotten rid of them"; years later, however, I realized that this effort probably has no end and that I will keep discovering new ones. How do we go about it? The first step is honesty with oneself: when I am debating someone, do I genuinely treat it as a real possibility that I might be wrong and the other person might be right? Not in some abstract, hypothetical sense like "we are all fallible," but do I actually allow for it in the specific discussion at hand? Another fairly clear sign of dogmatism is being more certain of a conclusion than of the reasons supporting it. How often do we see someone defend a thesis with a particular argument, and once that argument is refuted, instead of pausing to reflect and reconsider, immediately and frantically cast about for anything else to prop up that thesis?

On similar principles, compulsory school attendance ensures highly effective, across-the-board indoctrination in statism: children are legally required to be exposed repeatedly and over many years to state propaganda. On parents who resist, the state sics child protective services; and if they stand their ground, their children can be taken away (and indoctrinated anyway). If any other actor behaved this way, we would quite rightly deem it utterly unacceptable; yet precisely because of the indoctrination we ourselves have undergone, we even accept it when the state tells us how to educate our children and—if we fail to comply—threatens to kidnap them. Yes, kidnapping—for that is what it actually amounts to (even though the laws—laws written by the kidnapper—naturally claim otherwise).

I consider state schooling to be the most powerful tool for building and cementing the power of the state. While the security forces enforce it, the educational system plants in all of our minds a host of exceptions to the general moral rules we otherwise live by. Taking someone's resources under threat of violence is wrong; yet when the state does it, we somehow excuse it because we have been told there is no other way. Forcing someone to instill certain values in their children under threat of kidnapping them is not merely wrong—we regard it as utterly reprehensible; yet let the state do the exact same thing, and we not only understand it, we typically approve of it. And no wonder, when from early childhood we are all told it is for our own good and could not possibly work any other way; what else is someone supposed to think if they do not want to spend hours wrestling with the topic? Unfortunately, similar—perhaps even more popular—myths surround the state welfare system as well; we will turn to analyzing and dismantling them in the very next chapter.

name: 9. The welfare system
text:
Pensions, unemployment benefits, welfare handouts of all kinds, and care for the poor in general are domains in which modern states are so heavily involved that many people now regard them as one of the state's core roles. Indeed, one often encounters the view that if the government did not handle any of the above—and if solidarity were not enforced by coercion—it would practically cease to exist. Because these views are so deeply entrenched in society, people frequently forget that government-run welfare systems are a relatively recent invention; in the past, all of these things functioned normally as well—only on a voluntary basis.

I categorically reject variations on the claim that "it wouldn't work"—above all because it already worked for hundreds of years, but also because if solidarity truly lies so close to people's hearts that they are willing to invoke it to justify having the government restrict their own freedom, I see no reason why they would need states and their laws to practice it.

A social safety net existed long before the state took on this task. Indeed, available sources show that the voluntary welfare arrangements of that era were likely relatively more effective than today's state system. Information on this subject is widely scattered across numerous historical sources, but excellent compilation works on charity—especially in the Czech lands and Great Britain, complete with references to the relevant historical records—were written by Hynek Řihák, founder of the Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk Institute. Anyone interested in the details can search online for his essays such as "Education for the Poor, or Let's Not Forget Charity," "The Not-So-Wild 'Wild' Capitalism," "Private Education in Great Britain, Child Labor, and the State in the 19th Century," "Voluntary Hospitals, Medical Care, and the State in Victorian Great Britain," "Self-Help Societies," or "An Outline of Charity in Victorian Great Britain—Almshouses for the Poor."

Although voluntary welfare took countless forms, it mostly consisted of various charitable societies, two types of which were most prominent. The first type were classic charitable organizations in which the wealthy banded together to support different groups of the poor. The second type were

local "social insurance societies," which worked by having a larger group of people join together and pay regular (relatively low) dues, so that whenever one of them ran into trouble, the society stepped in to help. In the vast majority of cases, such societies generated no profit and were owned directly by their members. Alongside these mechanisms, there were many others as well (which can be read about in the writings cited above).

In the past, people practiced solidarity voluntarily; today they are forced into it. What is the difference? First and foremost, the most important point must be stated: a state welfare system operates by first robbing and impoverishing people, and only then offering help. After all, no one except the state has the audacity to strip people of most of the fruits of their labor and then presumptuously tell them to their faces: "See, you don't even have enough to feed your children or buy bread in your old age. Be grateful that you get at least a meager pittance back from what the government stole from you."

The vast majority of the money the government collects for the welfare system is paid out in old-age pensions. In this connection, it is essential to realize that the state does not invest or grow those collected funds in any way; on the contrary, it skims off a sizable portion (even setting aside corruption and waste, it at least has to pay the army of bureaucrats who administer the whole thing) and merely redistributes the rest. It follows logically that if people saved for themselves the same money they pay to the state in pension contributions, they would be far better off. There are two main counterarguments. The first is that if someone saves in a bank, the bank could go bankrupt and wipe out their deposits. Certainly that can happen, but it can be guarded against: we can split our money across multiple banks, buy real estate, invest in stocks, or buy gold and hide it in a secret stash under the floorboards (none of these options offers 100% certainty, of course—but neither does the state, as evidenced by the steadily rising retirement age). The second counterargument claims that people are irresponsible and many would simply fail to save for retirement—and virtually the entire fourth chapter of this book is devoted to refuting it.

Another crucial difference between voluntary charity and a coercive state welfare system is that a government must, by its very nature, establish a uniform system applying to the entire country and all citizens, whereas the voluntary solidarity of free people operates in a much more targeted way. The advantage of decentralized charity is that it can take different forms in different places depending on local needs, unbound by universal rules that cannot, in principle, suit everyone. The charitable societies replacing social insurance mentioned above illustrate this well: associations of workers in riskier professions—such as miners—typically collected higher dues to provide for families in the event of a breadwinner's death, cover medical care, and so on. Central planning of a welfare system can never be that effective.

The targeted nature of charities and benevolent societies also does a far better job of preventing abuse of the system. With local charity, abuse was policed directly by those who contributed their own money; their incentive is incomparably stronger than that of bureaucrats tasked with guarding against freeloading on money that isn't even theirs.

State bureaucrats, and in general those who design and administer the welfare system, can afford not to care how long benefit recipients remain dependent on the state. By contrast, charitable societies have an enormous interest in seeing recipients get back on their own feet as soon as possible! The entire operation of a charity and the manner in which support is delivered are typically geared toward that goal. Benevolent associations that effectively functioned as unemployment insurance for their own members actively checked whether a recipient was looking for work and often covered related expenses (such as travel costs, retraining fees, and the like). Unlike the state system, voluntary welfare is often guided by the maxim that it is better to give a poor person a fishing rod and teach them how to fish than simply to hand them a fish.

An equally serious problem with the state welfare system is the notion that someone has a "right" to receive money from it. It is not hard to imagine the difference in attitude between someone who realizes they are living on charity (and is duly grateful for it) and someone convinced that they are "entitled" to the state funds they live on (where gratitude is often replaced by resentment that they aren't getting more—after all, they have a "right" to have others provide them with a "dignified life"). In this regard, I find it strange to hear the views of certain—especially right-leaning—people who rail against "welfare leeches and lazy freeloaders living off handouts" while adding in the same breath that "the state has to provide some kind of welfare system," which necessarily implies someone's "right" to benefits. How can anyone declare receiving welfare benefits a right and yet criticize people for exercising that "right"?

A common argument for preserving the state welfare system is that we are civilized people and, as such, cannot simply let the poor starve to death. Even leaving aside that voluntary charity can prevent this too (and deliver help in a better-targeted way), I would like to point out that in our part of the world, practically no one is actually in a financial situation that forces them to go hungry. Not even people living on the streets—homeless people, some of whom receive no state support at all (I personally know several, and there are certainly quite a few overall)—starve, because begging for enough money for a full day's food in a busy spot takes at most a couple of hours (and with a bit of luck, just a few minutes).

A very interesting question is why that is. Roughly a hundred years ago, the poor went hungry (often even with state support), and five hundred years ago even the middle class frequently suffered hunger; today, however, in the "Western world," not even the homeless and beggars go hungry. Naturally, this is because society as a whole grows richer over time. What every other person owns today was a luxury of the wealthy only yesterday. For instance, among people living below the so-called "poverty line" in the United States, 76% have air conditioning at home, 66% have more than two habitable rooms per person, 97% have at least one color TV, 62% have satellite or cable television, 75% own a car, 30% own two or more cars, 73% have a microwave, 50% have a hi-fi stereo system, 33% have a dishwasher, 99% have a refrigerator, and 46% live in their own home. A hundred years ago, such living conditions would have been considered sheer luxury. When we ask why things we now take for granted were once viewed as luxuries, the answer is obvious: greedy, selfish entrepreneurs, in their pursuit of profit, made all these goods affordable to ordinary people so they could sell to them and grow rich—and for that, they are routinely condemned. This growth, which has helped the poor so tremendously, was certainly not brought about by robbing the rich; on the contrary, robbing the rich effectively slows it down (one can only guess how many failed businesses could have survived and made all the conveniences listed above even more accessible to the poor had they not been crushed by taxation and state regulation).

And it is an indisputable fact that the more the state takes care of the poor and declares that to be its role, the less citizens care for them (why should they, when the state is already doing it—and with their money, no less?), something Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk already grasped back in 1919: "In place of humiliating charity, we put social duty today." When evaluating the necessity of a state welfare system, I ask the reader to consider not only what is visible at first glance, but also what fails to function or never comes into existence because of it—and above all, the inevitable, unintended consequences of granting someone a "right" to other people's money simply because they are poor. Much the same applies to the "right" to medical care, which we will examine in detail in the next chapter.

name: 10. Healthcare
text:
Healthcare is one of many sectors so heavily regulated that it is de facto run by the state and subject to central planning. The government accredits hospitals and individual doctors, thereby determining how many hospitals of each kind will exist and where; at the same time, it regulates virtually everything that happens inside those hospitals, meaning that even when it does not own them outright, it effectively controls them more than their private owners do. And as so often happens with such things, almost no one today can even imagine healthcare without the state.

The most common argument against free-market healthcare is that medical procedures are so expensive that only the richest of the rich could afford them, and that without the state it would be impossible to provide care on the current scale. Frankly, I do not understand how anyone can reach such an absurd conclusion. After all, the state does nothing other than forcibly take resources from people and then use them to pay for their medical care. It possesses no arcane magic by which it can mysteriously multiply the collected funds and buy something people otherwise could not afford. On the contrary, it possesses certain—far less magical—tricks for squandering a considerable share of the money it collects. The state certainly does not provide some greater volume of healthcare that people could not pay for themselves (in fact, they are paying for it themselves through the state). Rather, rampant waste, pervasive corruption, the impossibility of economic calculation (explained in detail in the second chapter), and the need to pay an army of bureaucrats to administer the entire redistribution scheme substantially reduce both the scope and quality of available care.

How, then, could an ordinary person afford healthcare when surgeries cost tens or hundreds of thousands, and there are even procedures and treatments costing millions? Would everyone have to keep that kind of money stashed under the mattress for a rainy day? Of course not. The insurance model—including health insurance specifically—has worked successfully for hundreds of years without the state. The principle is simple: when someone occasionally needs expensive treatment, they do not need to save the entire sum themselves. It is more than enough for many people to pay a relatively small amount on a regular basis so that whenever one of them falls ill or gets injured, their treatment is covered from the shared pool. None of this requires the state at all.

And what about those who simply do not pay for insurance and cannot pay out of pocket? Do we leave them to die in the streets? Well, for them, charity is the last resort. Historically, charities typically assessed to what extent the afflicted person was responsible for their plight, how much control they had over it, what their current means were, and how costly the needed treatment was. Understandably, help went primarily to children and the infirm, rather than to layabouts and reckless freeloaders (though even they sometimes received aid, especially if it was not very expensive). More on how charity operates without the state can be found in the previous chapter. So the answer to the question is that we would likely not leave the sick to die in the streets when they had little control over their situation (children, the elderly, the infirm, the disabled), though we might be less indulgent toward irresponsible slackers. Why this approach is desirable is explained in the fourth chapter of this book.

There is a well-meaning ideal that goes something like: "Equal healthcare for all." I am afraid most of its proponents defend it only because they have not thought it through to the end. "Equal healthcare," after all, can mean anything from a state-of-the-art clinic staffed by top specialists to bloodletting in a filthy basement; the phrase says nothing about the actual level of quality, only that it must be the same for everyone. Most people mistakenly assume that in practice this means decent, average-quality medical care for all—their intuitive picture is that the average person will get roughly the care they could afford on their own, while the rich will chip in extra for the poor to bring everyone up to that average.

Yet almost nothing could be further from the truth! Out of the money collected, the state spends a large share on the salaries of bureaucrats who keep the whole behemoth running, as well as on corruption (which is an inherent feature of the state and bureaucracy, not something that can simply be "eradicated"). Whatever remains after embezzlement and bureaucratic payrolls is then spent desperately inefficiently due to the impossibility of economic calculation (see the second chapter of this book for details). The result is therefore nothing like "average medical care for all," but rather dismal, far-below-average care relative to the amount of money people are forced to pay—meaning that even the "ordinary person" politicians are so fond of invoking loses out. If someone objects that this is how it ought to be and that we should make do with less so that literally everyone can be treated regardless of whether they take any responsibility (keeping in mind that the "ordinary person" is not someone who couldn't afford care, as explained above), then I ask them: "Do you truly believe it is morally right for your children to receive worse healthcare just so a handful of irresponsible people can get the exact same treatment?"

Another—slightly less extreme—idea can be put this way: "Fine, not everyone has to have the exact same healthcare, but some basic level of treatment should be provided to anyone." Something along those lines can be achieved through voluntary charity (a fuller explanation is in the previous chapter). When the state tries to do it, however, it is never just a simple transfer of resources from everyone to the poorest; enormous amounts are lost along the way, and the rest is misallocated (see above). Once again, the state has no way to achieve this goal other than by degrading medical care for everyone else.

Another emotional argument, which often surfaces after the previous ones have been refuted, is that many ordinary people already struggle to make ends meet and therefore could not afford private health insurance. Beyond the fact that the preceding paragraphs already refute this, I would like to point out explicitly that these people have so little money precisely because they are taxed so heavily; the total tax burden in our country is so enormous that if we did not pay taxes, most of us would have several times more income at our disposal than we do today.

The huge problem in healthcare is not just the state-run payment system; it is also the mountain of laws and regulations that prevent entrepreneurs from finding effective ways to treat patients. A typical example is the requirement that every new drug must first go through a series of lengthy, expensive laboratory trials—and often animal testing as well—before the government allows it to be tested on humans; unfortunately, even the patients' own consent changes nothing, because at least a baseline level of safety must supposedly be guaranteed first. Surely such a regulation is right, isn't it? We don't want evil pharmaceutical corporations testing drugs on humans just to boost their profits, do we? Roughly 99% of people nod along to that. And who opposes it? Only a handful of crazy extremist libertarians defending individual liberty at any cost, no one else... So everything is fine, right? Oh, I almost forgot, there is one more group: people who are currently dying of a disease for which someone is developing a drug, except the drug still has to jump through regulatory testing hoops, so they are simply out of luck. Are we seriously letting them die just to make sure some pharmaceutical company doesn't profit from testing drugs on people—even when those people consent, the drug could help them, and they desperately want to live? And that is to say nothing of all the people dying today from diseases that could have been successfully treated years ago if the state had not slowed down pharmaceutical development. Lest there be any misunderstanding, let me add that I categorically oppose testing drugs on people without their consent. Similar legislative obstacles arise, for instance, with the ban on selling organs: it is supposedly inhumane for someone to sell a kidney, so apparently it is better for one person to die rich of kidney failure while the other ends up on the street.

Regulations are defended on the grounds that without them, any butcher could call himself a doctor and any lice-infested basement could call itself a hospital. Sure, in principle they could. The question is who would go to such a doctor, and which insurance company would contract with him. Without regulations, precisely those doctors and hospitals that people actually want to use would thrive, while the unsuccessful ones would go bankrupt. A frequent question is how anyone could tell whether the person standing in front of them actually graduated from medical school or got their education from binge-watching Dr. House. Well, apart from the fact that the insurance company would likely verify this already (since it wants to keep its clients and has no interest in contracting with doctors and hospitals it knows nothing about), it would hardly be difficult to open the website of the school—or a certification body, as discussed in more detail in chapter eight—where the doctor supposedly studied and check even their academic record. Today such a service does not exist mainly because doctors and hospitals are accredited by the state; if they weren't, demand for it would emerge, followed naturally by supply.

One sometimes encounters the objection that in certain countries healthcare is "more market-based," yet the results are not very good. The catch, however, lies in misunderstanding the greatest advantages of the free market, which include not only free competition, but above all the freedom for people to try whatever they see fit, to fail if they get it wrong, and to prosper if they succeed. Being "more market-based" therefore does not just mean having more private providers and fewer state ones, but above all freedom of enterprise. Nor is the sheer number of regulations what decides; what matters is what is regulated and how. Even a healthcare system in which every provider is private—yet the state dictates who may practice and under what conditions—can (depending on those conditions) fail more catastrophically than a system that at first glance appears far more heavily regulated.

Many people think about key sectors—such as healthcare—along these lines: the state may mismanage them now, but if only we had more moral politicians, wiser advisors, more capable bureaucrats, and a more efficient public administration, everything would work well. Leaving aside the fact that democracy leads to nothing of the sort (as can be observed all around us), even if that were somehow achieved by a miracle, things might improve somewhat, yet in principle a state system can never be as efficient as a market solution (see the second chapter). The same applies to the management of public spaces, the subject of the next chapter.

name: 11. Public spaces and freedom of speech
text:
All around us there are spaces with no private owner, because the state acts as their administrator—squares, parks, forests, meadows, fields, rivers, and various buildings, as well as roads and paths. In this chapter we will consider whether free people could manage such land better. The one aspect we will set aside for now is transportation and all transit functions of public spaces (especially roads and paths); the entire next chapter is devoted to that major topic.

I consider the most serious reason why the state (and by the state I include municipalities) should not own any land to be the very same as in every other domain in which the state intervenes: maintaining public space costs money; no government of any state is—or has ever been in all of history—productive, so the funds it spends it must, and always has had to, loot from its subjects. I view robbery as a deeply immoral act, and behind every state-owned square, forest, building, and road we see around us lies stolen money. For this reason, I cannot agree to the state managing public spaces.

And as is usually the case on the free market, morality goes hand in hand with efficiency, so there are practical arguments as well. One of them was presented by the well-known scientist Dr. Garrett James Hardin in his famous essay "The Tragedy of the Commons," in which he compares a private owner's treatment of his own pasture with people's treatment of a state-owned one. A landowner grazes only as many cattle on his meadow as it can sustain without being ruined, so that it can continue to support him. By contrast, in sixteenth-century England there were common pastures onto which anyone could drive their cattle; the inevitable result was that people overgrazed them, rendering the land unusable for that purpose.

Many other thinkers have built on this insight in their work. For instance, my favorite author, Murray Newton Rothbard, in his book "The Ethics of Liberty," describes the tragedy of the commons as follows: "If the state owns land and allows individuals to use it freely, this naturally leads to overuse of that resource and to waste." In practice, this problem can be seen in the state management of unique natural landmarks (there is little incentive to guard them properly), certain protected animal species (if private individuals were allowed to profit from them, it would be in their own interest to protect them from poachers), and the pollution of rivers and air (more on that in the thirteenth chapter).

However, I see an even bigger problem than overuse: deciding how a given space should be used. If the state owns an empty lot, how does it decide whether to turn it into a park, a shopping center, a playground, or a parking lot? A group of bureaucrats makes some kind of decision. Their motives may vary—from taking a bribe, to living nearby and needing a place for their own kids to play, to a crystal-clear conviction that a park is the very best thing for local residents. Ultimately, the sincerity of a bureaucrat's motives does not matter: he cannot know what is best for people, even if he happened to care. Even the results of a referendum would only show how many people voted for each option, without capturing how strongly anyone wants one option over another. Moreover, such a vote can yield completely different results depending on how wide a geographic area is included (commuters might prefer a parking lot, while local residents might favor a park). Once the project is built, the state runs it with public funds, and without economic calculation (see the second chapter), there is no yardstick to tell whether it is doing good or harm.

When these plots of land are owned by entrepreneurs, however, what will their goal be? To generate profit, of course. And the highest profit comes from building whatever people are willing to pay the most for—which is precisely what they want most. Entrepreneurs therefore have an incentive to build exactly what people desire (even though they do so for purely self-interested reasons). Much like bureaucrats, entrepreneurs cannot know in advance which use of a given plot is best; so different people try different things, and many varied projects emerge. The better a project satisfies consumer preferences, the more money it makes; bad projects lose money, which quite naturally leads to their being replaced by projects that people actually want.

A common objection is that if we leave all land to private owners, they will build shopping malls, parking lots, and office buildings everywhere, leaving no parks or playgrounds. Similarly, after the Velvet Revolution, many people (including politicians and economists) argued that grocery stores had to be centrally planned, or else food shops would become scarce because entrepreneurs would open nothing but boutiques instead. In reality, however, demand always calls forth a corresponding supply; that holds true for grocery stores as well as parks. If there is sufficient demand for parks, parks will certainly be built. If people are not willing to pay for them, that means those parks should not exist, because people actually value something else more (whatever it is they are willing to pay for). This insight (explained more fully in the second chapter) is crucial because it applies universally. It is also worth noting that "demand for parks" need not mean only that people are willing to pay an entrepreneur admission to a park; it can equally take the form of enough neighbors pooling their money, buying a plot of land, and creating their own park there (unlike the state, however, they do not force anyone to chip in).

Private ownership of what are currently called public spaces solves yet another major problem. I imagine many readers, upon seeing this chapter's title, wondered what public spaces have to do with freedom of speech. Well, let us first look at the difficulties involved in arriving at a coherent definition of free speech. Virtually all states suppress freedom of speech: they typically ban either speech against the current regime, the promotion of other regimes, or both—often adding further prohibitions on top. The Czech Republic is no exception; promoting fascism or racism, for example, is illegal (I am certainly no racist, and as a libertarian I regard fascism as pure evil, yet I will always defend free speech even for those with whom I profoundly disagree). Even so, schools lie to us and claim that since the Velvet Revolution we have freedom of speech. That is simply untrue: although the current regime persecutes fewer people, even today certain public statements can bring down brutal state violence upon you and land you in prison (one can debate whether such laws are justified, but freedom of speech it most certainly is not).

Should everyone, then, be allowed to say whatever they want anywhere, or else it counts as oppression? At first glance it might seem so, yet that is not the case. It also depends on where they do so. Obviously, if Jehovah's Witnesses ring your doorbell and you do not invite them straight into your living room to preach about their faith, you are certainly not infringing on their freedom of speech. If, however, a law is enacted prohibiting Jehovah's Witnesses from evangelizing, that is a clear trampling of their freedoms. A well-known example is the man who, for his own amusement, shouts "Fire!" in a crowded theater and triggers a panic; many philosophers and thinkers have grappled with this, including the American judge Oliver Wendell Holmes, who concluded that the right to free speech cannot be absolute and must be qualified and tempered with regard to "public policy." The flaw in this approach is that, depending on how "public policy" shifts, freedom of speech can be stamped out completely (see totalitarian regimes).

What, then, is the moral as well as practical solution to this problem? Let each owner decide on their own property what may and may not be said there; no state-owned spaces will exist. And in the exact same way that everyone decides what people can and cannot say in their living room, an owner decides what people can and cannot say in their park. This solution is completely natural and fully consistent with property rights.

Some speculate that if free speech were left solely to landowners, it could lead to a flood of arbitrary rules and needless restrictions on expression. That, however, is exceedingly unlikely: if an entrepreneur opens his property (a parking lot, movie theater, park, public pool, etc.) to people in order to make a profit, it is not in his interest to impose absurd restrictions that drive customers away. Another concern is that certain opinions would remain banned—much as they are today. Yet that is completely unrealistic: whereas under a state all it takes is for the government to approve a ban, in a free society every single landowner would have to enforce it simultaneously. And even in the unlikely event that happened, proponents of the suppressed view could buy their own land where their own rules would apply.

The opposite argument holds that if the owner alone decided what could and could not be said on a piece of land, there would be plenty of places where people could say whatever they wanted. That is very likely. What would be wrong with that? Some people might promote ideas leading to violence, or outright lies. Certainly, that would happen from time to time; on the other hand, their opponents would have the opportunity to refute such falsehoods. Of course, that provides no guarantee that a clever manipulator won't win over the crowds—but as history shows, states provide no such guarantee either, and with a state there is the added danger that such a manipulator ends up inside the government itself, from where he has far greater power to silence his opponents by law.

Upon further reflection, we find that with the very same elegance with which freedom of speech can be defined through property rights, we can do the same for freedom of religion, freedom of assembly, the freedom to use one's own language, and so on. The rules in any space are always set by the owner of that place. It is simple and clear, with no need to draw arbitrary lines or enact universal statutes; above all, it is moral (everyone decides over what is theirs) and consistent ("fundamental human rights" are thus grounded in property rights, so they can never come into conflict with one another). Although in this chapter we examined the efficiency of managing public spaces as well as freedom of speech, religion, and assembly, the issue of freedom of movement still remains open; the next chapter, however, is devoted precisely to that—and, of course, to the statists' favorite question: "If there were no state, who would build the roads?"

name: 12. Roads and traffic rules
text:
Perhaps the most frequent question statists ask once an anarcho-capitalist mentions a stateless society is, curiously, not about courts, police, or the military, but rather: "And who would build the roads without the state?" Although this question is the butt of many libertarian jokes—which might suggest an obvious answer—I personally do not find the topic particularly easy to explain. Still, I will try to show why the right answer is: "Free people, ruled by no one, will build the roads—and far more efficiently than the state."

First, let us focus on the problem of state highways and intercity roads, whose construction and maintenance are so extraordinarily expensive today. The attentive reader can already guess that there are two root causes behind these problems: a lack of incentives and the impossibility of economic calculation.

One manifestation of this lack of incentives is pervasive corruption, which virtually wipes out market pricing and makes it possible for highway expenditures—running into the hundreds of billions—to vary several-fold from one highway to the next (at times, it is even cheaper to build in mountainous Austria than in the relatively flat Czech Republic, where wages are lower overall). The true market price of a highway is hard to even imagine, though it would likely be dramatically lower than today's costs (just for comparison, a square meter of Czech highway costs more than a square meter of an ordinary single-family house; covering an area with houses packed right next to each other, without yards, is cheaper than running a highway through it).

A manifestation of the impossibility of economic calculation is that no one really knows which routes justify building a highway for a given cost, nor how often it makes economic sense to repair roads given their usefulness and the cost of repairs. Not to mention that the state has no way of knowing whether we have too few roads overall (and which ones are missing) or too many (and which ones are redundant). Surveys of actual road usage cannot yield meaningful answers either, because as long as the maintenance costs of each particular road are completely severed from its use, prices cannot reflect the scarcity of resources; thus no one knows whether a driver currently using a road would still do so if he had to pay the market price for it (a fuller explanation of this phenomenon is in the second chapter).

Private ownership of roads solves both of the above problems very elegantly. Corruption is minimized because entrepreneurs guard their own money far better than bureaucrats and politicians guard state money (and if they fail to do so, they soon have no capital left to stay in business). The impossibility of economic calculation disappears entirely: a road that turns a profit is clearly beneficial, whereas a road that loses money is not beneficial in its current form (people derive less value from it than they would from the resources it consumes). Furthermore, these figures make it possible to determine how frequent and how costly the repairs on a given road ought to be.

The most common objection to private highways is that if their owners (or the owners of individual segments) jack up prices ad absurdum, people will have no choice but to accept and pay them. That might be partly true if no other transportation option existed. Yet that condition is almost impossible to meet, because in reality there is an alternative to every road—both in the form of other roads (even if it means a detour) and other modes of transport (railways, for instance, compete with an overpriced highway). If someone sets prices outrageously high, they will lose customers. And even if the owners of all transport routes between two points somehow conspired to raise prices, a new route could be built (cartels are generally unsustainable on a free market; details can be found, for example, in the chapter "The Waste Producer" of the fantastic book "Defending the Undefendable" by the well-known libertarian thinker Walter Block).

The only "advantage" the state holds over a free society in building highways lies in its power to expropriate land along a planned route. I put the word "advantage" in quotation marks because it is a very dubious one—first and foremost because the act of expropriation itself is profoundly immoral, amounting to the theft of land whose value to its owner is obviously higher than what the state is offering (otherwise, there would be no need to force the owner to sell by force). It might therefore seem that buying up land for highways would be too expensive under anarcho-capitalism. Without state intervention, however, the price would simply be the market price—completely natural—whereas with state intervention it is lower only at the expense of the owners whose land was expropriated! And if we recall the second chapter of this book, we realize that if land acquisition makes a highway so costly that it is not worth building (or forces it to take a detour), that means the land along the proposed route yields greater utility without the highway than with it. Thinking this through to its conclusion, we see that the dubious "advantage" mentioned at the start of this paragraph is actually a disadvantage.

I sometimes hear the view that private highways could probably work, provided they were not owned by too many different owners (since building a highway is no cheap undertaking, multiple investors and entrepreneurs would likely pool their resources to finance one), so that drivers wouldn't have to stop at a toll booth every few kilometers. The same argument is then commonly raised against private ownership of city streets: collecting tolls on every corner would inconvenience drivers and disrupt the flow of traffic. Of course, toll booths are hardly the only solution. Street owners could sell passes (much like highway toll stickers) or GPS beacons—or, if someone did not want a device in their car constantly tracking their location, chips scanned by readers only on the relevant streets—or cars could be equipped with a kind of "taximeter" activated and deactivated by external signals. All of these solutions (and the free market would surely invent many more) could operate in parallel, and most importantly, multiple owners of streets and roads could share a unified system, thereby lowering their transaction costs and offering customers greater convenience (so no toll booths on highways every few kilometers).

While it is reasonable to assume that highways and intercity roads would mostly be built by entrepreneurs for profit, for city streets and lanes one can expect that many would be owned by the owners of the adjacent buildings (a street can be built right alongside the houses, with no reason to sell it off and make residents pay just to pass through). Related to this is the concern that cities could become gridlocked because some owners might refuse to let outsiders' cars onto their streets. Well, some might indeed do so. However, the bigger a problem that became, the higher prices would naturally rise, which always increases supply—so owners who wouldn't bother letting outsiders' cars drive down their street for pennies might well find it worthwhile for a reasonable fee. Associations of street owners could also form with reciprocal transit agreements.

To the possible objection that prices for using homeowner-owned city streets would be too high (which, of course, no one can claim with certainty—nor the opposite), one can only reply that those prices would produce precisely the traffic pattern that yields the greatest overall utility to society. It is hypothetically possible (though there is no evidence for this, nor for the opposite) that city traffic would decline as a result—yet that would happen only if the actual value city residents placed on quiet streets exceeded the value drivers placed on driving through them (following the principle described in the second chapter).

One can also expect that road-use prices would vary by time of day: likely higher during rush hour (allowing road owners to prevent congestion) and lower during off-peak hours (attracting more customers). This would naturally motivate drivers to schedule their trips, whenever possible, outside peak congestion times. Likewise, people would have a stronger incentive to carpool—more passengers per vehicle—especially during rush hour when prices are highest. Many of the outcomes that tax-funded traffic experts strive for in vain today would be achieved by the free market quite naturally and spontaneously; moreover, on the market these goals are genuinely shaped by the public's wishes, as every driver and road owner registers their preferences with each transaction (unlike under state management, where the guesses of experts and bureaucrats about what people want can diverge dramatically from reality).

And what about traffic rules? They would always be set by the owner of each road. A very common objection here is that rules would vary from road to road. Yes, they might differ slightly, which—when it comes to minor details—is actually a good thing, as rules can be tailored to each specific road. The fundamentals (which side to drive on, who has the right of way, etc.), however, would be practically identical everywhere, because every road owner has a direct interest in minimizing accidents, keeping traffic flowing smoothly, and ensuring customers feel comfortable (nonsensical or overly eccentric rules would cost the owner profits). Examples of these same principles working today can be seen in the dimensions of credit cards or in barcodes. Even in the absence of government standards or mandates dictating the format of barcodes or the shape of credit cards when they were created, cards from different issuers are mutually compatible with card readers, and millions of businesses worldwide rely on just a few barcode standards. Nobody invents wild, incompatible rules, because doing so would hurt their own business. There is no reason to think traffic rules would be any different.

In closing, I would ask the reader to notice how many problems—ones that governments around the world have been fighting unsuccessfully for years—the free market could solve without spending taxpayer money on absurd social engineering, campaigns for alternative transport, traffic-calming schemes, and other regulations. Much the same can be said of the environment, whose stewardship we will examine in the very next chapter.

name: 13. The environment
text:
Environmental protection is one of the areas commonly cited as an example of where the free market supposedly fails, allegedly requiring state regulation. Unlike most state-regulated sectors, which spark heated debate and emotion, environmental protection is not brought up as often in discussions about anarcho-capitalism; as usual, almost everyone simply "knows" the state has to handle it because otherwise "it wouldn't work." Let us therefore think this topic through a bit more deeply.

Sometimes I ask myself how well the state actually performs its role as protector of the environment in practical terms—and unlike with other sectors, surprisingly, I cannot just look around at first glance and say it is doing a bad job. With environmental protection, it is not even clear what "doing a good job" means. It could mean completely untouched wilderness with people living in trees, or "sustainable development," or anything in between. The only sensible standard, then, is probably that nature should be shaped in the way that best suits human beings—and the best way to achieve that is the free market. We could stop right here by referring back to the eleventh chapter and stating that the state should not exist, and therefore should own nothing, leaving environmental stewardship on every piece of land to its owner; let us, however, examine the matter in detail.

Environmental protection illustrates—perhaps better than anything else—the absurdity of central-planning data-gathering methods based on the government polling people, letting them vote on issues, and the like. There are plenty of people in our population who, on the one hand, lament how nature is suffering, how evil industry is destroying it, how humans mistreat animals, and how big cities are swallowing up forests—and once they finish talking, go home to their heated city apartment, enjoy a meal of genetically modified chicken, wash it down with artificial, factory-made junk, take a hot shower, and go to sleep in a wooden bed. It is precisely such people who often skew voting outcomes by proudly backing the strictest possible environmental rules, failing to grasp that doing so does not merely restrict some "evil businessmen," but above all those businessmen's customers—namely, themselves. For this reason, democratic decision-making on environmental protection can end up working directly against the very people who voted for it.

But why would private landowners care about nature? Wouldn't they choose financial profit instead? Well, those two things very often go hand in hand. If someone owns a piece of nature that people appreciate, it is possible to earn money from it—and the more people value it, the higher the potential earnings. Many people might also buy untouched natural areas without any financial motive, purely for the sake of nature itself; enthusiasts can likewise pool their funds for such purchases through various clubs and associations. Moreover, the more "endangered" nature becomes and the scarcer unspoiled places grow, the higher their price will rise and the weaker the incentive to destroy them will be (see the first chapter).

One sometimes hears the argument that if nature reserves had private owners, no one could stop an owner from building a factory assembly line right in the middle of his pristine, beautiful forest. Theoretically he could do that, yet it is hardly likely. Anyone wanting a factory hall is generally after profit—and for that very reason has no incentive to build it inside a forest that others are willing to pay just to keep untouched (whether individuals, associations of people pooling their money, or an entrepreneur seeking to profit from a nature reserve). For an industrialist, it is generally far more advantageous to buy land with a lower market price (or a better location).

The same holds true for protecting endangered species. Because the state typically prohibits profiting from such animals (ivory being a classic example), the incentive to protect them is low, and poachers slaughter them indiscriminately (see the tragedy of the commons in chapter eleven). One example speaks for all: millions of bison once roamed America, forming the backbone of the culture and society of Native Americans whom the U.S. government wanted to get rid of. In 1871, Congress passed a law authorizing the wholesale slaughter of bison (any hunter could shoot any bison regardless of who owned it), which nearly drove them to extinction (by 1889, only 542 remained). Once that law was repealed, the "Society for Saving the Bison" and numerous private bison ranches sprang up. Today, bison are no longer an endangered species; their population is estimated at three hundred thousand.

Pollution poses a major environmental problem. Who will stop chemical and industrial waste from being dumped straight into rivers? The owners of those rivers, of course; they can sue whoever is polluting their river (how such legal disputes might work in a stateless society is described in the next two chapters). Even if a polluter bought the stretch of river where he discharges his waste, that still wouldn't solve his problem, because he would still be harming every owner of the river downstream, who could sue him or seek to defend their rights by other means; in light of that, building a treatment plant and not discharging pollutants looks like a sensible investment. A similar principle applies to air pollution.

But what about garbage? Without states, wouldn't we turn the planet into one giant landfill? When considering this, it is essential to realize that without states there would be no "public land"; every plot of land would have an owner who would suffer damage from illegal dumping. Waste disposal would therefore be operated by entrepreneurs, paid for this service by those who want to get rid of their waste.

In connection with waste, many object that the state supports and subsidizes recycling, making it indispensable. What is recycling actually good for? First, it reduces the volume of waste, and second, it conserves virgin natural resources. At the same time, however, the recycling process itself consumes resources (both natural resources and human labor and the like). How, then, do we find the right balance between what is worth recycling and what is not? Sharp readers probably already suspect that the answer lies in the first chapter of this book. Whenever it is cheaper to manufacture new products from waste than to dispose of the waste on the one hand and extract fresh raw materials on the other, that means recycling truly saves resources. When the reverse is true, it means the resources consumed by the recycling process are scarcer than the resources needed to dispose of the waste and extract new raw materials. In other words, recycling saves resources if and only if it is profitable—without any subsidies. State subsidies for recycling are therefore harmful and lead to waste.

Another popular topic is sustainable development. This doctrine preaches that we should not consume so-called non-renewable resources (or only on condition of full recyclability). People assume that a stateless society would not follow this maxim—though, for that matter, neither do existing states, even if one could argue that some governments occasionally make a partial attempt. Yet what is the biggest flaw in this doctrine? It completely ignores progress and innovation. It is not unlike a once-respected medieval theory about the maximum possible size of a city, which assumed the city would be supplied by horses hauling grain from surrounding fields: given the minimum acreage required to feed each person and horse, once the population passed a certain threshold, hauling distances would grow so great that the horses would eat all the grain they were supposed to deliver. The doctrine of sustainable development is just as short-sighted and naive in assuming that humanity will keep obtaining energy in the exact same ways. Take oil, for example: it is running out—thirty years ago it was supposed to run out in thirty years, today it is supposed to run out in thirty years, and thirty years from now it will probably still be supposed to run out in thirty years. All such forecasts look only at currently known oil reserves, ignoring the fact that scarcity drives up prices, which motivates entrepreneurs to search for new deposits. And they ignore altogether the possibility that, over time, oil might cease to be our primary fuel at all (just as coal once was). In the words of Professor Julian Lincoln Simon: "The Stone Age didn't end because we ran out of stones."

A similar issue is the clearing of rainforests. Thus far, it does not threaten life on Earth; if it ever began to do so, people would naturally be willing to devote their resources to finding solutions (planting new trees, conservationists buying up the relevant land, or whatever else works). Just because we can envision a hypothetical future crisis does not mean the government must regulate and tax us today; the closer we get to an actual threat, the more willingly people contribute funds voluntarily (which is already starting to happen—for example, billionaire Johan Eliasch bought a tract of Amazon rainforest to prevent logging). Not to mention that states "protect" us even from problems they do not yet know how to solve. Take global warming, for which we have been forced to pour vast resources into ineffective or even counterproductive measures (such as ocean iron fertilization, biofuel mandates that drive deforestation, planting monocultures, or electric cars in countries where electricity comes from coal), just so that "something is being done"—without properly analyzing the impacts and consequences beforehand.

History shows that attempts to solve "global problems" tend to be either ineffective, or aimed at something that is not really a problem at all—or both. Regardless of how many times someone has sounded the alarm in the name of "saving the planet" and how many times people have been forced to finance "solutions," such efforts have only rarely produced even modestly meaningful results; far more often, it turned out we had merely squandered resources. The free market, by contrast, has repeatedly demonstrated its ability to solve problems (for example, through the mechanization of agriculture or the replacement of coal with oil as a transport fuel).
