In conclusion, let me note that when it comes to caring for the environment—just as in every other sphere of human activity—we have two choices: let free people decide for themselves what they truly want and express their preferences on the free market, or hand decisions over scarce resources to governments and their experts, who are incentivized to view issues one-sidedly in order to satisfy a political mandate, even if only an implicit one (see the "Climategate" affair). I leave it to each reader to judge which is better. And in the very next chapter, we will finally arrive at one of the fundamental differences between anarcho-capitalism and minarchism (the theory advocating a minimal state): private versus state justice.

name: 14. The Judiciary
text:
The judiciary, security forces, and defense against external enemies. We have finally arrived at the most interesting and also the most controversial topics in this book. Not only do most people refuse to entertain even the hypothetical possibility that these could exist without states and their governments, but these are also the areas that highlight the disagreements between anarcho-capitalists and minarchists (advocates of a minimal state). In this chapter, we will focus on courts and the judicial system; for now, however, we will set aside the question of how to take someone to court if they refuse to cooperate, or how to compel them to respect a court's ruling—that is covered in Chapter 15.

Why replace state courts with private ones in the first place? There are two fundamental reasons: in the hands of the state, the judiciary is both immoral and inefficient. The immorality lies, as always, in the fact that governments finance the courts through taxes collected under the threat of violence; everyone is forced to pay whether they want to or not, which is unethical and unacceptable. The inefficiency can be seen in how the courts themselves operate: judges often make utterly absurd rulings, frequently placing the letter of the law above its spirit and almost always above the wishes of the disputing parties; no one is held accountable for judicial errors (unless malicious intent can be proven); and it is not unusual for court proceedings to drag on for many years (while almost nothing can be resolved in less than several months).

Right at the outset of defending a free judiciary, I think it is important to mention that the ideas presented in this chapter certainly do not describe some untested theory. Many examples of well-functioning non-state courts can be found. Even setting aside anarchist societies such as medieval Iceland or Ireland, where there were no state courts at all, there are numerous examples of private justice operating alongside state courts. For instance, the Law Merchant (Lex Mercatoria), which emerged in England due to the inability of state courts to resolve merchants' disputes, had no backing from state power, and the decisions of merchant courts were not enforced by violence; yet—or perhaps precisely for that reason—it proved so successful that over time it became internationally recognized law. Maritime law underwent an almost identical development. From modern history, one can point to the rapid rise of arbitration firms in the United States, which have settled millions of disputes; even though their rulings were entirely non-binding legally until 1920, their services were widely sought after and used.

These examples clearly refute the fairly widespread myth that a judicial system is useless without a coercive apparatus to enforce its rulings by force; demonstrably, that is simply not the case. Why? There are many reasons. First, there are "punishments" other than violent coercion (for example, merchant law was enforced through ostracism: others refused to do business with a merchant who ignored a court's ruling, effectively destroying his livelihood; today, information spreads very efficiently, making ostracism arguably far more effective than in the past, when an ostracized person could solve the problem simply by moving far enough away). Second, violent dispute resolution is generally expensive; it can often be far more advantageous for both parties to turn to an arbitrator voluntarily—and abide by the ruling—than to enter into open conflict (especially when the arbitrator finds a sensible compromise). Third, there may be disputes in which not even the parties themselves are entirely sure who is in the right and genuinely care about finding the truth; in such cases, a wise judge can easily help without any use of force. And fourth, an arbitrator may uncover a solution to the problem that suits both sides, one they simply failed to reach on their own for various reasons. I am certainly not arguing that all conflicts could be resolved solely by courts without enforcement agencies backing up their decisions; I am merely pointing out that even courts whose rulings are not enforced by violence can resolve disputes on a massive scale to the satisfaction of the parties involved.

Who would appoint judges in a stateless society? The answer is simple: arbitrators would be "appointed" by the people themselves simply by requesting their services. Anyone whom both parties to a dispute agree upon could serve as a judge—whether it is a totem-carving grandfather from Canada settling a neighborhood dispute in a village, or a renowned corporation with decades of experience in adjudication conducting a complex arbitration between two other giant corporations. On the free market, demand for such services would give rise to firms making a living precisely by resolving disputes.

So anyone can be a judge. But when a dispute arises, how do the conflicting parties agree on which arbitrator will settle it? Well, first of all, there is a huge category of cases in which this problem will likely disappear altogether: disagreements arising from an existing contract. In a free society without a centralized judiciary, we can assume that every contract will include a clause specifying which arbitrator will handle any disputes relating to that agreement—this avoids trouble at the cost of minimal effort. For more complex contracts, an arbitration firm can manage the process comprehensively, from drafting the agreement to resolving any eventual disputes. When no contract exists and a dispute arises spontaneously, two possibilities remain: either both parties have an interest in reaching some kind of settlement (because fighting would be expensive and risky), in which case they agree on an arbitrator acceptable to both; or at least one party has no interest in a peaceful resolution, which we will address in Chapter 15.

The most common—albeit very short-sighted—objection to such a system goes something like this: "And what is to stop private arbitrators from deciding the dispute in favor of whoever pays more?" The answer is very simple: the main asset private arbitrators live on is their reputation. As soon as they lose it and prove to be bribable, people will stop seeking their services. The opinion of disinterested observers determines a court's credibility, which is critical to its survival. By contrast, the incentives for corruption are far higher in the state sector, where a corrupt judge can hand down one dubious ruling after another, yet unless someone practically catches him red-handed taking a bribe, he remains a judge and people simply have to entrust their cases to him. The fact that private arbitrators are far harder to bribe than state judges is best demonstrated by the fact that for hundreds and thousands of years people have turned to them with confidence and paid for their services, even when they usually had the option of using the state's supposedly "free" courts.

A private court's good reputation naturally rests not only on impartiality and incorruptibility, but also on its efficiency, reliability, speed of decision-making, and customer service. Unlike state courts, whose tax-funded income is guaranteed and cannot be lost—meaning they hardly care how customers perceive their services—private arbitrators must work hard to keep their clients and attract new ones. There is no reason why competitive pressure to lower prices and improve service quality should not exist in the free-market provision of justice just as it does elsewhere.

Despite all these undeniable advantages of independent arbitrators over state judges, one crucial question remains: under what laws will private arbitrators adjudicate when there is no uniform state legislation? Why, under whichever laws suit people best—that is how things work on the free market. Each of the millions of entrepreneurs who decide to make a living as independent judges will have their own vision of what the law "ought" to look like. Some will declare in advance the legal code they intend to apply, others will rely on customary law, still others will adopt a system of precedent combined with wise arbitrators, or someone might come up with a blend of the above or something entirely new. Those whose methods satisfy people will prosper; the rest will go bankrupt.

But won't complete chaos reign in the judiciary if every arbitrator rules according to different laws? Here again, we must remember that the solutions that succeed on the free market are precisely those that suit people best. In a society plagued by legal confusion, there will likely be demand for standardization, which will create a corresponding supply: groups of judges will unify their laws and procedures in an effort to gain a competitive edge over others and attract more clients who have no desire to learn a different set of rules or laws for every dispute (or every contract they sign). We can expect that in the end only a few time-tested frameworks will remain, changing only minimally when customers' needs require it; after all, history shows that having too many disparate ways of resolving disputes does not become a problem in a free-market judiciary.

This method of lawmaking has one fascinating consequence: rules emerge precisely as the people affected by them wish. There is no need to pay (potentially corruptible) legislators to forcibly impose their idea of law on society; there is no need for the farce called "democratic elections," in which we try to guess which political party will keep at least a fraction of its promises. People can decide on the laws simply by creating them and by supporting those judges whose legal rules suit them—directly by paying them to resolve disputes.

One frequently hears the objection that a stateless judiciary would end up with laws rigged solely in favor of the rich and powerful, leaving the "ordinary person" with no chance of obtaining justice. Few things could be further from the truth. For a harmful law to take hold in anarcho-capitalism, a large number of independent judges would have to start enforcing it, and people would have to tolerate it at least to the point where it wasn't worth their while to switch en masse to other arbitrators; when the rules of justice are set by the state, however, the consent of just a handful of (often corruptible) individuals is enough to pass such a malicious law.

Although the idea of privately provided judicial services is therefore not as absurd or crazy as it might seem at first glance, we have so far avoided examining cases in which at least one party refuses to cooperate and has no interest in an amicable settlement. What then? We will find the answer to this interesting question in Chapter 15.

chapter: 14. The Judiciary
name: A Free Judiciary and the Non-Aggression Principle
text:
Chapter 3 of this book discusses the non-aggression principle (a legal system based solely on property rights), whose "validity" in anarcho-capitalism I assume (by validity here I do not mean unconditional observance by everyone, always and under all circumstances, but merely that most conflicts will be resolved roughly in accordance with it). Despite this, in Chapter 14, where we examined courts and dispute resolution, the non-aggression principle was not mentioned at all. This subchapter is intended for those who find that odd, and in it I will try to clarify the connection between property rights and a free judiciary; it is not exactly light reading, however, so anyone who does not wish to delve into this topic (which I include only for the sake of completeness and rigorous argumentation) should feel free to skip it.

From the previous chapter, it follows that private arbitrators on the free market decide disputes in whatever way best suits people. At the same time, throughout the book I take property rights as my starting point. Aren't these two lines of thought inconsistent? Not if it turns out that free-market arbitrators will typically rule in accordance with the non-aggression principle. As it "happens," the entire history of private justice shows that they do indeed rule this way; almost all known human societies in which free, stateless courts operated (examples of which can be found in the previous chapter) were governed by natural (property) law roughly along the lines of the non-aggression principle, or something very similar to it. This fact suggests to some extent that property rights may actually be "hardwired" into our brains in some way, as already mentioned in Chapter 3 (while there is probably no way to prove such a thing conclusively, this observation can be taken as a meaningful clue). Historical experience also gives rise to the expectation that since private judges have so often ruled roughly in accordance with the non-aggression principle, they would continue to do so; yet on its own, history does not explain why this is the case, which is what I will attempt to explain in this subchapter.

Every one of us has probably heard the saying: "One person's freedom ends where another's begins." Personally, I am not very fond of this vague cliché, because it is actually a tautology that holds true under all conditions. After all, even the freedom of concentration camp guards ended where the freedom of their prisoners began. For that statement to make sense, there must also be an unspoken assumption that the boundary of freedom lies "in the middle" between those concerned. In that case, it becomes a very noble idea. Let us now look at it from two different angles.

First, let us compare it with the non-aggression principle. Clearly, it does not contradict the principle, given that a legal system based solely on property is completely non-arbitrary and does not grant anyone a priori more authority than anyone else, so the boundary of freedom between any two individuals under this principle is always right "in the middle." Of course, one can imagine other legal concepts that do not contradict the thesis that one person's freedom ends where another's begins (expanded with the premise that the boundary must lie "in the middle"), yet such concepts are highly unsystematic and, moreover, conflict with property rights.

Second, let us compare this thesis with the decision-making of free judges. As noted in the previous chapter, the impartiality and neutrality of these courts form the very cornerstone of their existence. If a private arbitrator is not impartial, people will stop using his services. And what is impartial adjudication if not an effort to draw the boundary of freedom between the disputing parties as close to the "middle" as possible? That is precisely what private arbitrators will try to do.

These two perspectives on the same issue partly explain why free judges mostly strive to rule in accordance with property rights. Why is the explanation only partial? Because, as noted above, there are still other legal concepts that are consistent with seeking the boundary of freedom "in the middle" between disputing individuals, yet contradict the non-aggression principle. Consider an imaginary legal system that includes the non-aggression principle, plus an "extension" obligating everyone to care for their parents in old age; such an idea may be noble, yet it conflicts with property rights and requires initiatory violence—that is, aggression against anyone who refuses to obey this "law." However, opinions on such modifications to law based on the non-aggression principle vary widely; everyone would prefer to enforce different ones. If an arbitrator adopts something of the sort, his rulings begin to diverge from those of others, putting him at a competitive disadvantage and potentially costing him customers (see the previous chapter). The further he strays from property rights, the more his rulings will differ from those of other judges, because the non-aggression principle is a kind of minimal subset of rules that can be said to apply equally to everyone (and by which a judge therefore rules impartially).

An objection to such reasoning that one occasionally encounters can be put roughly like this: "And where is the guarantee that the courts will actually recognize the non-aggression principle? What if a market demand arises for the mass trampling of property rights?" Of course, no such guarantee exists. Although history shows that this does not happen in free societies, it cannot be guaranteed with certainty that the future will not be different. Yet what guarantee does the state give us that it will not become a totalitarian regime? None either. There is, however, one difference: all of history is full of examples where the state actually did just that. Moreover, the absence of such a rigid guarantee in anarcho-capitalism brings an additional advantage: the non-aggression principle is not an absolute dogma that people must follow no matter what (which is how states try to present their laws); if a judge finds a strict application of property rights inappropriate in some specific case, he can simply rule otherwise (and if people consider the ruling wise, the judge will gain customers, whereas otherwise he will lose them; in this way—unlike state judges—he bears full responsibility for his decisions).

I hope that after taking all of the above into account, it is no longer such a mystery to the reader why courts in free societies have mostly followed the non-aggression principle, or some very similar concept. For the same reasons, property rights can be expected to be respected in any civilized society not corrupted by the state. Today, however, it is the state that handles the enforcement of court rulings whenever at least one party to a dispute refuses a peaceful resolution; therefore, in the next chapter we will focus on how this area, too, could function without state intervention.

name: 15. Law Enforcement
text:
The previous chapter dealt with a free judiciary; it showed why private arbitrators resolve disputes more morally and more efficiently than state judges, yet it focused solely on dispute resolution as such—leaving aside the enforceability of court rulings. Enforceability is crucial especially in cases where someone commits a crime and knows full well that any court would find him guilty, giving him no interest in arbitration whatsoever. The aim of this chapter is to explain how an anarcho-capitalist society could deal with such wrongdoers.

Most states use the police for these purposes. What is wrong with that? Besides the two usual arguments—that it is neither moral (the police are paid with money seized by force) nor efficient (the free market can allocate resources for policing better than the state—see Chapter 2)—there is one more fundamental reason why police power, the monopoly on violence, should not be entrusted to the state: history shows that whenever things go wrong and a despotic tyrant rises to power, this force is invariably turned against the state's own citizens. Even so, most people argue against putting armed forces in private hands by claiming they could be abused against the population, despite our knowledge of anarchist societies (medieval Iceland and Ireland) in which nothing of the sort happened on a mass scale even once over many hundreds of years of existence. By contrast, history is full of cases of massive abuse by state security forces, and it is practically impossible to find any inhabited territory under state rule where this has not happened repeatedly over such a long time horizon.

We can assume that by no means everyone will want to rely solely on their own abilities if they become the victim of a crime; in fact, assuming that such people will not be in the majority is hardly a bold guess. Demand for protection against criminals creates supply; entrepreneurs will be able to profit by offering people the services of private security agencies to assist them if they fall victim to an aggressor. Payment for such services could be either on a per-incident basis or via a regular subscription fee. These security agencies would likely employ both detectives to investigate crimes and armed mercenaries trained for direct confrontation with criminals.

So what happens if, for example, someone robs a client of such a security agency? The first problem is finding the perpetrator. Detectives begin investigating and gathering evidence. If they fail to find anyone, the victim might—depending on the terms of the contract—receive compensation from the security agency because it failed to perform the job it was paid for (this service is not unlike theft insurance). If the culprit is caught, what happens next depends on how he responds. If he surrenders and agrees with the victim on restitution, the matter is settled. However, if he objects (he might claim he is innocent, for example, or admit his guilt while calling the victim's compensation demands absurdly high), the security agency refers the entire matter to a private arbitrator (see Chapter 14), who decides the case. If the accused submits to the verdict, all is well. If he refuses to comply, the security agency compels him by force (in this case, however, it is not initiatory violence, since it is directed against someone who first violated the victim's property rights).

I imagine most readers have already thought something along the lines of: "Why would an agency turn to an arbitrator when it could just force the alleged perpetrator to cooperate with violence and save on court fees?" Well, that line of reasoning assumes that using violence is cheaper than settling through an arbitrator, which is hardly likely. Even if a private judge's fee on the free market exceeded a mercenary's pay, there are still a number of other factors that make violence expensive: even a trained mercenary can hypothetically be overpowered and killed by his target (especially if the target expects an attack); a violent confrontation could injure bystanders (potential or even current clients of the security agency); someone might seek revenge on behalf of the targeted person (potentially causing further losses); and last but not least, by carrying out extrajudicial killings, a security agency will make many enemies and earn a terrible reputation. A good reputation is vital for such a company not only so that people will buy its services, but also because it makes its work much easier when disinterested bystanders cooperate in tracking down criminals (if the public views a security agency as a genuinely just organization pursuing criminals, it will clearly receive far more assistance in such efforts than if people perceive it as a bloodthirsty mafia). Moreover, clients of a security agency typically do not want the death of the person who wronged them; far more often they want restitution, which simply killing the criminal does not provide.

We must also bear in mind that while all the above arguments apply to people who are not clients of any security agency, there is an even stronger deterrent regarding everyone else (who may well make up the majority): if a security agency tried to take out a customer of another agency, an armed conflict could easily break out, costing both sides money. War is expensive (especially for someone paying for it out of pocket rather than out of taxes), and waging one just to avoid paying an arbitration fee would be absurd.

Each security agency will therefore likely have standing contracts with arbitrators. In the event of a conflict between two clients of the same agency—or between one of its clients and someone not protected by any agency—one of the judges contracted by that agency will decide the case. If a dispute arises between clients of two different security agencies, it will be decided by an arbitrator contracted by both companies involved (and if no such common arbitrator exists, they can agree on one, which is still far cheaper than war).

People often ask for guarantees that the largest security agencies will not band together and take over the entire society. Of course, that cannot be guaranteed. Yet what guarantee is there that any given state will not turn into a dictatorship? None either—and how many times has that already happened! Still, there are many factors working against a stateless society being conquered by its own security agencies. First, a corporation large enough to have the potential to enslave a sizeable territory is usually run not by a single person, but by many shareholders. Second, it would not just be a matter of subjugating "ordinary people," because such a territory is also home to many economically powerful enterprises (which—across all industries combined—likely outnumber security agencies), and they can defend themselves effectively: even if combat is not their primary business, they can hire mercenaries. Not to mention that in an anarcho-capitalist society, "ordinary people" too will far more often be armed, making it much harder to subdue them by force. Moreover, the remaining security agencies that do not side with the "bad guys" will stand in the front line against the aggressors—for what better advertisement could a company in this industry wish for than thwarting such a threat? And what if, despite all that, everything failed and society were taken over by a few power-hungry corporations? Well, then our fates would be decided not by a handful of politicians as they are today, but by a handful of shareholders; the most catastrophic possible outcome is the emergence of a monopoly on violence—that is, a state.

So far we have looked at cases where a crime has already occurred; but how could crimes in progress be stopped? Suppose a mugger attacks an innocent person on the street while a patrolling mercenary from a security agency is standing nearby, not knowing whether the victim is a client of his employer. What happens now? The victim can call out to that patrol officer for help, thereby entering into a verbal contract with the security agency. But what if the attack is already well underway and the victim is unconscious? Will the private officer intervene without being asked? Most likely, his employer will instruct him to do so. First, he cannot know whether the person in danger is in fact a client; if it turned out that he was, the officer failed to step in, and the incident became public, people would quickly lose interest in that agency's services. Second, by rendering aid, the security agency can win a new customer, since someone whose property—and perhaps life—has just been saved will be far more receptive to signing a contract. Third, even if this particular mugging did not target a client of that agency, letting the robber get away means the next victim could be one of its clients, costing the agency additional resources. And fourth, it is reasonable to expect that security agencies will sign mutual-aid agreements to assist one another's clients in emergencies, because stopping a crime on the spot is cheaper than investigating it after the fact.

One frequently hears the objection that if security services are provided privately, the poor will not be able to afford them and anyone will be able to rob and murder them with impunity. The free market of medieval anarchist Iceland solved this problem with remarkable elegance: a wronged poor person—as the victim of a crime—had a legal claim to compensation from the perpetrator (in the case of murder, the heirs were compensated); he would transfer part of that claim in advance to a wealthy person who had the means to enforce it. Such an arrangement was advantageous for the wealthy man (who could collect compensation from the criminal even though he himself had suffered no harm) and for the poor man alike (since no one could harm him with impunity). We can expect that the poor could similarly sign contracts with security agencies that would take a share of the restitution in lieu of an upfront fee (the victim would receive less, but would gain protection against an aggressor that he could not otherwise afford).

Much more could certainly be written about private security forces, yet the aim of this book is to give the reader a coherent picture of the possible forms a free-market society might take, and overly detailed analyses would, in my view, detract from that. For anyone eager to explore this subject in greater depth, however, I warmly recommend my favorite author, Murray Newton Rothbard, who examined stateless security provision at great length in many of his works—as well as the earliest comprehensive writings on the topic, authored in the nineteenth century by the French free-market economist Gustave de Molinari. So much, then, for protection against internal threats; in Chapter 16—the final regular chapter—we will turn to defense against external enemies.

chapter: 15. Law Enforcement
name: Crime and Punishment
text:
Although Chapter 15 on free-market law enforcement by security agencies mentioned the compensation a criminal would have to pay his victim once caught, nowhere in the book so far have we discussed the punishment of those who violate others' property rights. I would like to remedy that in this chapter, in which I will offer several alternatives for how a free market in anarcho-capitalism might handle the problem.

Why several? Well, as we saw in the very introduction, no one can predict with certainty the free-market solution to any problem; if that were possible, there would be no need for a free market at all, since we could simply set everything up that exact way through central planning. As Chapter 2 explains, however, that is impossible, so we must settle for tentative expectations whose accuracy depends on how specific the problem is. Thus, while most anarcho-capitalist thinkers largely agree on how free-market education, healthcare, courts, or protection services might function, there are considerable disagreements when it comes to punishing criminals. Many theories have emerged in this area, three of which I am going to present here along with a fourth of my own. I leave it to the reader to judge which seems most reasonable—and I would also be glad if you propose another alternative and send it to me. I am certainly open to discussion; on the question of punishing criminals, I still have not found a solution I consider entirely satisfactory, though I am convinced the free market would come up with one.

Before I begin listing these theories, I would like to clarify the term "make restitution," as I will use it in describing them. Making restitution means two things. First, an attempt to restore things to their original state: in the case of theft, this means returning the property to its owner; if damage is done to non-unique tangible property (such as a fence), it means buying a new item of the same kind (or repairing it, if the result is identical or the owner agrees); if unique tangible property (such as the Mona Lisa) or someone's health is damaged, the remedy consists of paying all costs associated with attempting to restore it to its original state (restoring the painting, treating a broken bone, and the like) as well as paying compensation, the amount of which is determined by a judge based on an estimate of how much of the original value was lost (to the victim) or what the victim had to endure (pain or permanent damage). In borderline cases, distinguishing between unique and non-unique property is up to the judge. Second, making restitution includes paying the costs of apprehending and prosecuting the criminal along with any court fees, plus compensation for the time during which the owner could not use his property (for instance, if someone breaks a programmer's hands and he cannot write code as a result, the offender should reimburse him—or his employer—for lost income).

The strictest of the theories holds that if someone violates another's property rights with proven intent, the victim is the only person who can judge how painful an injury the aggressor inflicted, and therefore the injured party alone determines the offender's punishment, to whatever extent he sees fit. In the case of an unintentional violation of property rights, the violator must make restitution. Personally, I consider this theory the least acceptable, because it allows draconian punishments to be imposed for trivial offenses.

According to another theory, an attacker who violated a victim's property rights to a certain extent must both make restitution and allow the victim the right to violate his property to the exact same extent that he previously violated the victim's. Thus, if someone steals a million crowns, he must return that million (and pay all costs incurred in recovering it as well as any losses the victim suffered from being deprived of the money) plus—as punishment—pay the victim an additional million. If someone breaks another person's arm, he must both make restitution and be subject to having his own arm broken in return (or reach an agreement with the victim to spare it by paying further compensation on top of restitution—as punishment).

The mildest theory, by contrast, holds that in every case the aggressor should simply make restitution and nothing more. His punishment consists in the extra expenses, since he would have to pay court costs, the costs of his own prosecution, compensation for the time the victim was deprived of the use of his property, any damages for pain and suffering, and so on. Of all the approaches, this solution strikes me as the most natural; still, many might object that it perhaps makes life a bit too easy for criminals.

The approaches above can be combined in various ways. For example: if someone intentionally violates another's property rights, the victim should be able to choose between receiving full restitution or violating the aggressor's property rights to the same extent. For property damage, the differences will be minimal (if someone took a million, the robbed party either demands that million back or takes a different million from the thief; the main difference is simply that full restitution also requires the aggressor to pay court costs, additional damages, and so on). A more interesting situation arises when someone harms another person's health. In that case, the victim can either ask for standard compensation, or—out of a desire for revenge—choose to inflict the same harm on the aggressor; yet there is also a third possibility: the victim can opt to violate the aggressor's rights to the same degree he violated the victim's, not with the aim of maiming him, but to demand payment in exchange for refraining from doing so—which could amount to more than what the victim would win through standard compensation (or the attacker refuses to pay, prefers to endure the injury, and the victim gets nothing). In the event of an unintentional violation of property rights, the offender would simply have to make restitution.

All of the examples above implicitly assume that the victim of the property-rights violation survived. But what if the victim did not? In that case, the victim's claim against the attacker passes to the heirs (which, of course, need not mean only family members—especially not if the murderer is among them), who sue the aggressor in the victim's place. This is another reason why the theory that the attacker should merely try to make restitution seems inadequate to me: if someone kills your child, the worst that can happen to him is having to pay you a lot of money. Under my theory, you can choose whether you prefer compensation or punishment (either you can kill the perpetrator outright, or devise virtually any other punishment for him, since he will very likely accept it over death).

Wondering why the word "prison" has not appeared once in this chapter so far? Well, that is because even though most states are so fond of using prisons as a one-size-fits-all tool for punishing offenders, I consider this method to be probably one of the stupidest ever invented. A criminal's stay in prison brings no financial benefit to the victim—at most a sense of satisfaction from revenge, which could be achieved far more easily (and cheaply, especially for taxpayers who had nothing to do with the crime). True, the criminal usually suffers in prison, which may deter him from future crime, yet deterrence can be achieved through other forms of hardship; locking someone up with other criminals and forcing him to live in such select company gives him ample opportunity to adopt their moral values as his own, not to mention learning plenty of new and useful tricks from seasoned, experienced offenders to improve at his "profession." And finally, there is "everyone else," who had absolutely nothing to do with the crime yet are forced by the state to pay for a punishment that neither they nor the victim chose. It is easy to imagine that for a vast number of crimes, the victim would prefer generous financial restitution over revenge, the perpetrator would likewise prefer paying over being locked up, and citizens would gladly avoid footing the bill for keeping criminals behind bars. Yet why choose a solution that would suit everyone involved when we already have another—far worse, but endorsed by politicians and bureaucrats as "tried and tested"?

Moreover, even in a stateless society, imprisoning offenders is not ruled out entirely. For example, if someone inflicts an injury on you with serious permanent consequences, under most of the theories above you have the option of inflicting the same injury on him in return. But if you offer him the choice of instead letting you lock him up for a few years in a prison you build on your own property, hiring a guard for him, feeding him, and providing his basic necessities, he will probably agree. This raises an interesting question: how many people would voluntarily choose that option (instead of, say, collecting compensation, or—if they truly craved revenge—doing something to the perpetrator in return), when it would bring them nothing but expenses and no return whatsoever other than a private zoo with a prisoner in the backyard? Something tells me there would not be many, if it were their money, their land, their headache, and their lost income. When "society" pays the bills, however, it is all too easy to throw money around in the name of the "greater good."

Although there is a vast array of ways a free market in an anarcho-capitalist society could solve the problem of punishing offenders (and I hope to hear about some new possibilities from my readers), I consider it virtually certain that the outcome would not be as senseless as the system we see around us today. After all, if prisons were to operate at all in a stateless society, inmates would likely be required to work, with the fruits of their labor divided between the victims and the prison company; yet such details are very hard to predict, because millions of entrepreneurs operating in a free market almost always come up with a better solution.

name: 16. The Army
text:
In this chapter, we will tackle what is probably the most difficult topic—namely, defending a stateless territory against an external aggressor. We can assume almost with certainty that such an aggressor would be a state, because since the dawn of history, free people ruled by no one have never attempted to conquer a large territory and subjugate its population. From time immemorial, wars have been the business of governments and rulers, never of their subjects—who nonetheless always bear the consequences and suffer for their rulers' decisions, at most being persuaded from time to time, at their own expense, through mass propaganda that they actually want war. Throughout this book, I have always offered two reasons why any given area should be managed by free individuals rather than the state: morality and efficiency. Nothing changes when it comes to morality; extracting funds from subjects for national defense by threatening them with violence if they do not pay cannot be called moral by any stretch of the imagination. Worse still, in the hands of politicians, "national defense" very often degenerates into "national offense," even if it is never called that (virtually every state has a ministry of defense and probably none has a ministry of attack, regardless of what those ministries actually do in practice). The death toll of all wars in the past century reaches roughly three hundred million; all those lives were destroyed by states—the very institutions supposedly here to keep people from slaughtering one another in anarchy—and their armies.

But what about efficiency? Although great anarcho-capitalist thinkers typically credit the free market with its usual superior efficiency even in running a military, I cannot agree with them on this point. If we pause to recall why free-market solutions are so much more efficient than state ones, we see that the main reason is the vast number of entrepreneurs, each trying to satisfy customers in the way he thinks best, with those who succeed turning a profit while the rest suffer losses (see Chapters 1 and 2). The market's huge advantage over the state is its self-correcting mechanism: the authors of bad solutions lose their capital and go bankrupt. While none of these principles cease to apply in military defense, a failed defense against an external enemy—who must necessarily be someone who disregards the non-aggression principle (otherwise he would not be an aggressor)—logically means the end of the free market in that territory. It is therefore not possible to experiment "with impunity" across different solutions and separate the good from the bad through profit and loss, which is the alpha and omega of market efficiency. Of course, this in no way implies that a state solution is more efficient; in my view, it simply means we cannot assume the state is automatically less efficient than the market here, as major anarcho-capitalist thinkers typically do. Even the brilliant Murray Newton Rothbard, who examines national defense in considerable detail in his writings, argued for the market's efficiency over the state in this area without first addressing this objection.

I see the greatest weakness of an anarcho-capitalist society in its very limited ability to block the movement of enemy forces across its territory. States typically possess large stockpiles of heavy weapons and equipment developed specifically for warfare and destruction. Free people, whom no one forces to buy such instruments, will presumably have fewer of them (assuming the same total wealth in society); and even the limited equipment they do have cannot be moved freely anywhere without the consent of the respective landowners (and anyone attempting to force his way through risks resistance that takes at least time to overcome). While we can expect strong motivation to cooperate against a common enemy, it will never be as straightforward as in a state that owns the road network and whose citizens follow government orders rather than the non-aggression principle.

As for the total volume of resources that a country of a given population can invest in armaments, I see no clear advantage on either side. An anarcho-capitalist society will certainly be far more economically productive than a state (which is the central theme of this entire book), yet people will probably not be willing en masse to voluntarily sacrifice everything they own—including their lives—for war. Granted, except in extraordinary situations, they will not do so voluntarily for their government either, but a government has the means to conscript and compel them if necessary.

Conversely, the undeniable advantage of an anarcho-capitalist society is that while it may not be all that difficult to invade its territory, effectively governing and controlling it would be an extraordinarily difficult task. When the army of one state occupies the territory of another, the defeated government surrenders and the existing power structures begin enforcing the conqueror's will. The invader immediately gains effective control over the population, because the people were already registered, monitored, tax-paying, and accustomed to obeying government orders; all that changes is who issues the commands—someone else simply takes over the pre-existing apparatus for forcibly subjugating dissenters. Nothing of the kind exists in an anarcho-capitalist society. The conqueror confronts not compliant masses, but individuals for whom no one can speak or negotiate—and who, moreover, often speak a language the invading soldiers do not understand. Not to mention that free people, without state regulations and gun bans, will likely be far better armed. To govern such a territory by conventional means, the aggressor would have to build all power structures from scratch, including registering the entire population and forcing them to obey laws that contradict everything they have ever known and grown used to—all despite a language barrier and weapons in the hands of free individuals who, unlike citizens of states, are accustomed to solving their own problems. Of course, an invading army could resort to brutal coercion, wiping out cities and killing inhabitants of the conquered territory on sight; yet once that becomes known and the defenders realize they have nothing to lose upon encountering a foreign soldier, the invaders will practically find themselves in a shooting gallery (bear in mind that for every invading soldier there will likely be several armed residents of the attacked country—and they will most likely shoot on sight).

Great Britain learned at least twice in history that the difficulty of subjugating a stateless society is no mere theory. Conquering the much smaller and weaker Ireland took Britain several centuries, because the Irish had no state or power structures to transmit orders to the general population. The English could not grasp that without any form of state, the Irish warriors who signed treaties with them could speak only for themselves; they could never bind any other group of Irish people. The British ran into a similar problem during the conquest of Africa, when they tried to subjugate the territory of the Igbo people (spanning between seventy and eighty thousand square kilometers, roughly the size of the Czech Republic); its inhabitants lived in genuine anarchy (and in accordance with several libertarian principles), having no chiefs or rulers whom they were obliged to follow. Governing (as opposed to merely overrunning militarily) so small a piece of land proved harder for the British than subduing all of India, where they ruled for centuries with relative ease simply by passing orders down to the ruling Indian princes, who in turn enforced them on their subjects.

"Well, sure," many readers may now be thinking, "but in the end the British conquered the Igbo territory anyway, and Ireland too, so anarchy can't be all that viable after all." True enough, most historical anarchist societies did indeed perish by being conquered by some state—yet we must remember that the exact same fate befell most states. Sooner or later, a larger and stronger empire came along and crushed and occupied the smaller, weaker one. All the analyses above of the strengths and weaknesses of states versus stateless societies in war assume a conflict between two roughly comparable adversaries. When we consider a fundamentally lopsided conflict, however, the social arrangements on either side are probably irrelevant to the outcome. If we imagine a war between the United States and the Czech Republic, for example, the United States will almost certainly win, regardless of whether either side is anarcho-capitalist or a state.

But what is the real reason no one is attacking the Czech Republic right now? Presumably, none of the governments of larger and stronger states have an interest in our territory. Whenever such an interest is strong enough, a pretext is always found (and international treaties will not change that, since they have been broken since the dawn of history). Would establishing anarcho-capitalism provide such a pretext? In my opinion, no one can answer that question with certainty. Either a larger and stronger country would ruthlessly seize such a territory, or it would not. Either way, even if an invasion occurred and succeeded, the anarcho-capitalist society would simply end up as a state again—nothing worse could happen. The absurdity of arguing that we need a state because, in the worst-case scenario, anarcho-capitalism might end up giving us a state hardly needs further elaboration.

Moreover, even if an anarcho-capitalist society on some small territory proved indefensible in practice, there would be no reason to discard the entire concept as unworkable. It would mean only that it probably cannot withstand overwhelming odds—something a state generally cannot do either. The inability of a small territory to hold out says nothing about the defensive capabilities of a vast anarcho-capitalist country.

Finally, it is also possible that if anarcho-capitalism proved viable in some territory over time, it would give citizens of all states a compelling reason to strive for the same system; if such efforts succeeded on a broad scale, our world could reach a point where defense against external enemies is no longer necessary. After all, a world without states is also a world without wars. To be sure, local conflicts would still flare up here and there, yet as long as they had to be paid for out of the pockets of those waging them, they would hardly have the potential to escalate to the monstrous scale of state wars.

name: Myth Busting
text:
In this bonus chapter, we will examine several widespread fallacies that come up constantly in discussions about a stateless society. Typically, they contain an implicit assumption that is cleverly hidden beneath the surface and, at first glance, appears true. The task of this chapter is to expose those assumptions and refute them.

I cannot begin without mentioning a brilliant French thinker and economist who accomplished this task masterfully back in the first half of the nineteenth century: none other than Claude Frédéric Bastiat. He dedicated his essay "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen" precisely to debunking popular fallacies. Reading it, one can scarcely help marveling at how many issues that troubled people two hundred years ago remain relevant today—and how many errors, refuted for two centuries, politicians still manage to repeat and voters still manage to believe. I warmly encourage everyone to read "That Which Is Seen, and That Which Is Not Seen"—it is a short essay freely available online; an hour or two is enough to read it, and in that time you will gain more—and better—knowledge than by taking many an economics course, let alone a political science one. In this chapter, however, I will not dwell on fallacies already demolished two centuries ago; in any case, Bastiat did it far better than I ever could.

A massive fallacy that, in my opinion, deserves closer examination is the widespread confusion between price and cost in sectors almost entirely controlled by the state. Carl Menger—one of the founders of the Austrian School of economics—already refuted Ricardo's cost-of-production theory of value back in 1870 (according to which a good's value corresponds to the effort expended to produce it) and replaced it with the subjective theory of value (the value of a good equals the highest price someone is willing to pay for it). Yet just as that refutation did not stop communists from flocking to Marx's doctrine built upon that discredited error, today's general acceptance of the subjective theory of value (at least intuitively) does not stop people from slipping back into the cost theory when evaluating state actions. For instance, when the state pays amount X to build a road, people assume the road's value is X (provided there was no embezzlement); of course, that is false, because the value of the road is still equal to the amount people would have been willing to pay for it voluntarily—which could easily be less than X. In that case, the road should never have been built at all (or should have been built more cheaply, even if to a lower standard). The exact same reasoning shows up in healthcare (people assume the price of a medical procedure is fixed and equal to its current cost; they never consider that it could be lower and that the procedure ought to be performed more cheaply, even if at lower quality). Many people imagine that capitalist healthcare would look virtually identical to state healthcare, only financed differently; yet that notion (and all others like it) contradicts the subjective theory of value and substitutes the long-discredited cost theory in its place.

Another fallacy, growing from the very same roots, is often expressed by the objection: "If the state didn't pay for this or that, people wouldn't voluntarily spend money on it." Even leaving aside the fact that such claims typically project present conditions onto an anarcho-capitalist world (for example, the claim that the state must provide pensions because people wouldn't manage on their own, since almost no one saves voluntarily for retirement today—overlooking that people don't save voluntarily largely because the state is already doing it for them), there do remain certain goods for which it is genuinely true that without state funding, people would not be willing to pay for them on the current scale. But what does that actually mean? Only that people value other things more than those goods. Why? Because they would rather spend their money on something else. Thus, when the government forces people under threat of violence to pay for something they would not pay for voluntarily, it leaves them worse off than they would be without that coercion.

Opponents of anarcho-capitalism very frequently raise the following argument: "What guarantee is there that one of the security agencies—or some other powerful corporation—won't take over the whole society and enslave everyone?" Well, of course there is no such guarantee. Then again, there is none in any state either. Moreover, even if that happened, such a corporation would hold a monopoly on violence and would effectively become a state. So this "catastrophic failure" of anarcho-capitalism simply means it turns into a state. "Sure," many reply, "but not all states are alike; a corporation that takes over an anarcho-capitalist society could be unbelievably cruel and evil." Indeed it could—yet why do so many people assume that shareholders of large corporations will always do their worst, whereas politicians in government (whichever government it may be) will not? Just take a look at the moral character of our current politicians! How likely is it that a corporation's shareholders would be any worse?

Another favorite rhetorical absurdity is comparing anarcho-capitalism against a nonexistent, unattainable mythical utopia with zero flaws, rather than comparing it to an actual alternative (even a theoretical one). Countless times I have taken part in or witnessed debates on anarcho-capitalism in which its advocate is backed into a corner by opponents and forced to defend a stateless society in utterly preposterous scenarios (the most extreme one I ever witnessed even featured a homemade black-hole generator). As soon as he admits that the outcome might involve some injustice or even someone's death, anarcho-capitalism is immediately ridiculed and dismissed as flawed—as if states never caused anything of the sort, as if the modern world had no wars killing people by the millions, as if gulags and concentration camps had never existed, as if there were no evil under the state. We must always remember that probably no anarcho-capitalist considers a stateless society perfect and flawless—only the best realistically possible. We do not claim that eliminating coercive governments will solve every problem in the world; only that there will be fewer of them.

Whenever a widespread problem arises in a state-controlled society, people tend to call on the government to fix it. Something is wrong? Just ban it—nothing could be simpler. Few stop to consider what side effects such a ban will have. And even on the rare occasion someone thinks through the direct consequences of a ban itself, they seldom factor in the cost of enforcing it. If we spend resources enforcing a ban, those resources will logically be missing elsewhere. Calling for state intervention should always be the absolute last resort (ideally so far down the list that it is never reached).

Moreover, we can see quite a few cases in our society where the problem itself is created by some law or regulation. A classic example is when states first force their citizens to accept unbacked fiat currency and grant banks the privilege of issuing that currency, only to later have to invent further "regulations" to restrain banks in doing so—even though it would be more than enough simply to repeal the laws causing the problem in the first place. By the way, who guessed why the word "regulations" is in quotation marks? Well, if something is regulated by one law while a second law weakens the first, it makes sense to call the second law deregulation, not regulation. Among other things, it follows that the so-called "deregulation" of banking—so often blamed for the economic crisis—was in fact regulation (laws mandating acceptance of the national currency and enabling banks to issue it are regulatory; laws that curb those privileges are deregulatory; ergo, weakening those curbing laws constitutes regulation).

Given that hundreds of similar myths have taken root in the public consciousness, I could go on for a long time; and since new ones keep popping up, I created a section on my website dedicated to debunking widespread misconceptions. You can check it out at ankap.urza.cz; you can expect me to expand it over time (at least, that is what I have been doing so far).

I cannot close this chapter in any better way than with the words of the well-known Czech chef Zdeněk Pohlreich. Although his views are at times socialist, he captured brilliantly why people are so prone to rejecting any change (which of course includes moving from the state to anarcho-capitalism): "You know what most people consider the worst thing about any change? That afterward, things are different." And indeed—how many arguments against anarcho-capitalism amount, de facto, to nothing more than saying that things would be different?

name: Conclusion; and What Next?
text:
With this conclusion, I would like to bring the main part of this book on anarcho-capitalism to a close. My primary goal in writing it was to introduce this school of thought in a nutshell, to inspire readers to think, and to show not only what anarcho-capitalism is, but also what it definitely is not. I do not consider it terribly important whether all of you agree with me; what I do hope is that your agreement or disagreement stems from deeper reflection rather than a mere first impression. And if, on top of that, reading this book has made the worldview of at least some of you even a little more liberty-minded, then the time I spent writing it has borne double fruit—and there is certainly no need for you to immediately label yourself an anarcho-capitalist. I can well understand that many people view the state as indispensable in certain sectors while unnecessary in others, which is completely reasonable; even if I have not convinced you, say, that state courts, police, and the military are unnecessary, there is no reason to dismiss the idea of free-market schools or money along with them. And if you are dissatisfied with everything I have written, please try to take this book at least as inspiration to come up with something better.

From time to time I am asked how I actually envision "introducing" or "establishing" anarcho-capitalism in practice. The answer to that question does not belong in a description of a stateless society, so you will not find it in any of the previous chapters; I will, however, use this space to address it. The only way to transform our society into an anarcho-capitalist one is to persuade enough people of the beauty of freedom and the inviolability of property rights as the path to it. The more of us who embrace this idea, the more voices there will be spreading it; at the same time, in democratic elections people will cast their votes for more liberty-minded political parties, which can repeal both the laws that restrict us most and those through which the state effectively spreads its propaganda, especially within the education system.

Make no mistake, I am certainly not an advocate of "change from above" (by politicians); I strongly believe the initial impetus must come "from below," yet real change requires multiple forces working both "from below" and "from above." We need theorists, debaters, thinkers, and think tanks, but also populists, charismatic figures, entertainers, and punchy slogans; we also need rebels, the underground, civil disobedience, and the gray economy—yet likewise lobbyists, diplomats, and, unfortunately, politicians and their political parties. I do not claim that politics will save us, for I myself consider it filth; still, even the contents of a stinking cesspool have to be handled from time to time, even if one gets dirty doing it. Personally, I am very glad others do that work for me, because I have no wish to sell my own soul; yet I will not condemn them, even though it seems almost every successful political party is eventually corrupted by its own power—until then, at least, it can serve the cause of liberty.

And once the state, as a result of this painstaking work, has shrunk enough to allow private actors to compete freely—without regulation—in every area where it interferes today, people will be able to see for themselves that it is not actually needed. And once there are enough such individuals with meaningful strength, they will have the ability to defend themselves adequately against an aggressive state. By that time, however, the state will already be weak and—compared to today's—relatively peaceful, so it will probably not even try to subdue dissenters by force, but will allow them to coexist alongside it without infringing on their property rights. I personally would consider that an absolute victory; I have no need to destroy the state, I only want it to leave me (and everyone else who wishes the same) in peace (even if such a voluntary "state" would essentially be a private company).

I have just outlined how, in my view, anarcho-capitalism could be put into practice. I would also like to add a few explicit words about how it definitely should not happen—or rather, how it cannot possibly be done. In principle, the path to anarcho-capitalism cannot be a revolution or a coup; if a revolutionary seizes power, he can establish almost any regime, except one that fundamentally rules out anyone holding power in the first place. Anarcho-capitalism certainly cannot be imposed by force, because you cannot compel people to value their freedom if they do not do so out of their own conviction. People can be forced to build a brighter tomorrow under communism, to conquer living space for a master race under Nazism, to abide by election results in a democracy, or to obey a monarch's every word—but they cannot be pushed into freedom by violence, because such means directly contradict the end. Even if someone seized the government by force, abolished it, and relinquished power, another government would soon be set up unless the people themselves wished to have no government; and if the revolutionary forbade them from doing so, he would become the ruler and the state himself. Initiatory violence is not only an unsuitable and morally unacceptable means, it also cannot lead to the goal, because it stands in sharp contradiction to it. Revolution is definitely not the way—and least of all a bloody revolution.

Although this conclusion marks the end of the regular chapters—each of which examined how an entire sector currently held by the state would look on a free market—there are still other areas of state influence that I believe deserve our attention. The next few supplemental chapters will be devoted to them, in which I will try to cover several controversial topics that frequently come up in discussions about a stateless society.

Although I have a soft spot for analogies, I have tried to avoid them throughout this book because they are often misleading and imprecise; here, however, I cannot resist adding one final postscript.

Imagine a country where people live free of restrictions; they exchange goods with one another voluntarily, and no one interferes in their trade. Then along comes a group of "bright minds" who build a giant tunnel right in the middle of the territory. On one side of the tunnel they gather the consumers; on the other side, the producers. The "bright minds" listen to the consumers' wishes, alter them as they see fit, collect money from the consumers, and send it through the tunnel to the producers, who manufacture goods according to specifications that also come out of the tunnel. All exchange of certain types of goods outside the tunnel is banned. Both producers and consumers are thus reduced to an undifferentiated mass; individuality is lost. Consumer desires are filtered through an intermediary; the goods emerging from the tunnel are distributed among consumers independently of what anyone paid, guided instead by the will of the "bright minds" and by who shouts loudest about how much they need them. Meanwhile, on the other side of the tunnel, producers make no effort to tailor their services to consumers (they don't even know consumers' preferences anyway), catering only to the wishes of the tunnel administrators.

It is sheer folly, then, to look for the root cause of people's dissatisfaction—compared to being able to trade directly—in the fact that the "bright minds" occasionally pocket a bit for themselves (embezzlement), that some money gets lost along the way in the tunnel (high bureaucratic overhead), that a producer or consumer sometimes bribes a tunnel administrator for special favors (corruption), or that the tunnel administrators are incompetent and unhelpful (the normal state of civil service). Those problems certainly exist, yet they are secondary. Even if you managed to fix or eliminate every one of them, the outcome would barely improve. The primary problem, of course, is the very existence of the tunnel itself—which turns individuals with distinct preferences into a gray mass, destroys vast amounts of information, and brings nothing but waste and ruin.

Above all, however—and I consider this far more important—it is unethical for someone to dictate to another person with whom and on what terms he may or may not trade, or to seize his resources under threat of violence. Anyone who does so commits aggression against him, which means nothing but evil. The state is evil.

chapter: Other Areas of State Influence
name: Drugs
text:
Many people hold the belief that state regulation of narcotics—based on outlawing the sale and possession of many of them—protects society from drug addicts and the crime associated with them. Here I will try to show why this reasoning is so astonishingly misguided that even its exact opposite can be called a true statement.

Personally, I consider the main reason the state should not interfere in who ruins their own body, to what extent, or with which drugs to be the simple fact that the body does not belong to the state, but to the individual in question—and therefore he, not the state, should have the right to decide what to do with it. When the government and the police stop him from doing so, they grossly violate his rights. Although I find this argument so fundamental that I need no other, I fully understand that many readers think more pragmatically and care primarily about the overall impact on society; that is precisely what I would like to examine in this chapter.

When assessing the effects of banned narcotics on their users, we must first realize that addictive substances are not automatically bad for everyone, because only the individual himself can decide what brings him how much benefit; trying to force our own definition of happiness in life onto others simply does not work. Some people will not touch even alcohol or coffee (and if we adopted their standards, we would have to ban those drugs too); most people have no problem with alcohol and coffee, yet object to many other drugs; some also view marijuana or even LSD as acceptable; and there are those who use cocaine from time to time but would not touch heroin for anything in the world. There is no universally correct threshold that we can prescribe for everyone. What gives us the right to judge which of these approaches is the only valid one? Yes, some are riskier, but by that logic we might just as well ban mountaineers from climbing peaks because many misjudged the risks and paid with their lives.

As part of the war on drugs, school anti-drug programs often make no distinction between different illegal narcotics—essentially describing the effects of heroin and implicitly attributing them to all banned substances—while the dangers of legal drugs are typically glossed over in such talks (hence the odd phrase we hear so often: "alcohol and drugs," as if alcohol weren't a drug at all). I am certainly not claiming that taking drugs is safe, since using any addictive substance always carries risks; on the other hand, I do not think it is wise to lie to children about the effects of narcotics, because once they uncover that lie with respect to less risky drugs, they may well lose respect for the truly lethal ones as well.

Although there are many ways to evaluate the danger of individual narcotics (such as the degree of physical harm to the body, how quickly addiction forms, the strength and type of dependence, difficulty of quitting, and withdrawal symptoms), I have bad news for all respectable folks who would "never touch drugs, though they enjoy a good beer": alcohol ranks among the more dangerous narcotics (even though worse ones exist), and compared to LSD, for example (which, by the way, is non-toxic, so you cannot even overdose on it), alcohol fares catastrophically poorly by almost every conceivable metric. In reality, the differences between individual drugs are vast (and I am not talking about the dubious division into "hard" and "soft" drugs). Just as many people drink and smoke without drinking themselves to death or dying of lung cancer (though that does happen), it is equally possible to use most narcotics for decades without serious consequences. Some are extraordinarily fast to form a habit (heroin), while others are difficult to get hooked on (ecstasy); some cause physical dependence (nicotine), others psychological dependence (cocaine); some inflict severe harm on health (barbiturates), others negligible harm (LSD); and overcoming an existing dependence is relatively easy with some drugs (marijuana) yet extremely difficult with others (alcohol). While certain addictive substances can be considered a fairly reliable tool for slow suicide (krokodil), most drugs (LSD, alcohol, cocaine, caffeine, marijuana, ecstasy, tobacco, and many others) can be used over a lifetime (obviously with widely varying frequency depending on the user and the substance) while still living a long, fulfilling life. In theory.

Why in theory? Because in practice, many drugs are absurdly overpriced—their illegality drives prices several orders of magnitude above production costs. As a result, manufacturers and dealers, whose livelihood is illegal either way and who face prosecution regardless of the quality of their product, cut drugs with all sorts of junk and filler, making them even more dangerous. Even more importantly, addicts fall into financial ruin, from which they escape right back into the drug, shrinking their entire existence to chasing the next fix while their addiction deepens all the faster. In that state, many turn to crime, endangering others as well; yet were it not for the war on drugs—which multiplies drug prices by orders of magnitude—addicts would in most cases be destroying only themselves, much as we see with homeless people drinking cheap boxed wine. Please do not read this as a defense of people who rob others to pay for their next fix; I am not excusing them, merely stating that state repression makes the entire situation worse. If a dose cost just a few crowns, there would be no need to mug or murder for it—even a junkie has easier ways to scrape together pocket change; when, thanks to the state, an addict needs hundreds of crowns every day to feed his habit, he is far more likely to resort to violence.

I grant that beyond the direct threat of addicts committing robberies, there is another problem: drug addicts are on average far sicker than other people (both because of the narcotics themselves and because of their illegality, which drives up drug prices and plunges users into poverty, destitution, horrific living conditions, dirty needles, and the like). Everyone else then ends up paying for their healthcare; yet that is not an argument for drug prohibition (which only worsens the plight of addicts—and secondarily everyone else), but for free-market healthcare, which solves that problem (see Chapter 10).

Another serious objection raised by supporters of drug prohibition is the health of our children: if narcotics are legal, they could be sold near schools! True—yet they already are today; if a schoolkid wants a drug, he can get it, let us have no illusions about that. We can comfort ourselves by calling it a "system failure" and claiming "better policing" would solve everything, yet first of all that isn't true, and more importantly it doesn't matter right now; what matters is that it is already happening. Legalizing drugs might make them slightly easier to obtain, though the allure of forbidden fruit would vanish. Above all, however, responsibility for children would be placed back where it belongs—on the children themselves and their parents, whose job is to protect and educate them rather than relying on the state's illusion of safety (and absolving themselves of their own failures by blaming the state). Do we want kids to stay off drugs merely because none happened to cross their path yet, or because they understand why they should say no?

Sometimes we hear the fear that if drugs were legal, society as a whole would destroy itself and everyone would overdose to death; yet people can already do that with legal narcotics. It is absurd to assume that legalizing addictive substances would unleash a drug apocalypse, because most people simply have no desire to ruin their lives (and if they did, they could do so today). Moreover, pouring ever more money into the war on drugs has demonstrably failed to reduce the number of addicts in society, clearly showing that repression simply does not work. In Portugal, for example, drugs became a severe problem in the 1990s; huge numbers of people were dying of overdoses, and HIV infections kept climbing. In 2001, the Portuguese government legalized the use and possession of small quantities of all drugs (including heroin). The results? Within fifteen years, overdose deaths plummeted by a factor of twenty-seven (!), and new HIV infections leveled off.

The fact that Portuguese politicians decriminalized drugs once they came under public pressure shows they were well aware of what the war on drugs was causing—it simply suited them until they started losing political points (had they genuinely believed in the effectiveness of repression, they would merely have cracked down harder). Other countries are no different: politicians and officials handling drug policy know the data (not only from Portugal), yet have no interest in a real solution, because their careers depend on drug problems continuing to exist. This also ties into how the war on drugs actually began (I do not mean its main wave in 1971, but its very origins in the nineteenth-century United States). It had nothing to do with protecting the public; it was driven by lobbying (hemp competed with nylon in textiles and with wood pulp in papermaking) and racism (Asians typically used opiates, while South Americans and Africans used coca-based drugs; banning these substances made it possible to harass their users)—something that isn't even a secret, since back then it was not yet politically incorrect to proclaim it openly, and politicians did.

The war on drugs was not, is not, and never will be about protecting society (it demonstrably achieves the exact opposite); it exists solely for power. Those whose current careers depend on fighting drugs will never admit such a thing, of course—yet the Global Commission on Drug Policy, a body composed of former powerful officials who devoted their careers to the war on drugs but no longer make a living from it (including former presidents of South American countries, a former US Secretary of State, a former head of the UN, a former NATO Secretary General, and a former EU High Representative), openly declares: "The global war on drugs has failed, with devastating consequences for individuals and societies around the world."

Drug prohibition is the exact same nonsense as Alcohol Prohibition in the 1920s United States; the only difference is that it affects fewer people, so its catastrophic consequences are not visible at every turn. In a stateless society, however, one can imagine drugs being sold just like any other commodity, which would undoubtedly improve not only the purity of those substances—among other things, it would also spell the complete end of drug cartels, which are created solely and exclusively by the war on drugs. After all, what would be the point of smuggling or secretly manufacturing and stockpiling something that is freely available in stores?

chapter: Other Areas of State Influence
name: Weapons
text:
It is to be expected that in a stateless society, everyone would arm themselves according to their own judgment and financial means; private landowners could certainly set whatever rules they wished on their own property, including restricting the carrying of weapons, though such restrictions would only be local in nature. The idea that practically anyone could carry a firearm anywhere else is none too pleasant for many of us, because we have grown accustomed to regulations whose creator—the state—instills in us from childhood the belief that without it and its laws, society could not function and we would all shoot one another.
